HB 2257.digest: Shipping or Transporting Tobacco Products . Alternative nicotine products are removed from the definition of tobacco products prohibited to be ordered or purchased by mail or through the internet. "Alternative nicotine product" means any noncombustible product containing nicotine from any source that is intended for human consumption, whether chewed, absorbed, dissolved, or ingested by any other means. Technical and Administrative Changes to Newly Enacted Retail Services . The following technical and administrative changes are made to the retail services recently enacted under ESSB 5814: clarifies the types of activities that meet the definition of information technology services and investigation services for purposes of the retail sales tax; clarifies that temporary staffing services do not include direct hires or paymasters; clarifies that the following activities do not meet the definition of live presentation subject to the retail sales tax: classes provided by preschools; classes provided by elementary schools, secondary schools, and institutions of higher education as part of their accreditation; before and after school care provided in-person and on-site by elementary schools; presentations given by nonprofit organizations; musical, dramatic, comedic, or similar performances, including any incidental instruction; one-on-one instructional activities including tutoring, consulting, music lessons, and any ensemble or large group instruction; presentations given at the physical location of a religious organization; presentations where participants may join via internet or telecommunications equipment and are given at the physical location of the presenter during the real-time presentation; and youth camps. provides that if a person is unable to source advertising services to the local level due to a lack of information, the person must source the services statewide in a manner prescribed by the DOR; authorizes the application of the affiliate exclusion for customized software and customization of prewritten computer software; clarifies that the use of a digital automated service that is incidental to the underlying service provided by a business is not subject to retail sales tax if the underlying service is subject to any B&O tax classification other than retailing; imposes the use tax on all the newly enacted retail services except live presentations; and corrects statutory references, updates definitions, repeals obsolete language, and makes other changes to conform the newly enacted retail services with existing law. Exemption . Kindergarten through grade 12 (K-12) schools, school districts, and educational service districts are exempt from sales and use tax on all services recently enacted by ESSB 5814. Transition Grace Period . A transition period is established for taxpayers with qualifying existing contracts for service activities that have been reclassified to retailing activities. The transition period begins October 1, 2025, and ends March 31, 2026. Taxpayers with a qualifying existing contract may elect to treat the amounts received during the transition period as gross income subject to the retailing B&O tax and retail sales tax or the service and other activities B&O tax. If a taxpayer with a qualifying, existing contract makes no election during the transition period, the amounts received will be subject to the retailing B&O tax and retail sales tax. HB 2259.digest: Initiative and Referenda Filing Process . A sponsor of a proposed ballot measure must include in its initial filing with the Secretary a petition containing the signatures of at least 1,000 registered voters in support of the proposed ballot measure. The signatures must be accompanied by the individual's name, address, city, and county were they are registered to vote. The Secretary may not accept an initial filing that does not include such a petition. Prior to submitting the initial filing with the CRO for a certificate of review, the Secretary must verify and canvass the signatures on the petition submitted with the initial filing using statistical sampling or other techniques to verify whether the petition contains the required 1,000 or more signatures. Signature Gathering . A person may not pay or be paid for signature gathering on a pay-per-signature basis, but may provide or receive money or other consideration for signature gathering that is not based directly or indirectly on the number of signatures obtained. A person may bring a cause of action in the name of the state against a petition sponsor for a violation of the pay-per-signature prohibition within two years of the date of the alleged violation. Civil remedies, including penalties not to exceed $10,000 for each violation, may be awarded. Any judgment award in favor of the plaintiff must escheat to the state, but a prevailing plaintiff may recover attorneys' fees and costs from the defendant. If a cause of action is dismissed and the court finds that it was brought frivolously or in bad faith, the court may order the person commending the action to pay all reasonable attorneys' fees incurred by the defendant.

HB 2260.digest: A petition signature gatherer circulating an initiative or referendum must sign and date the declaration on each sheet of the petition. The petition signature gatherer must sign the declaration under the penalty of false swearing, which is a gross misdemeanor. The declaration requires the signature gatherer to swear that every signer reviewed the sheet and signed without any gratuity or promise of gratuity. As part of the declaration, the signature gatherer must also provide the signature gatherer's address and county of registration. For purposes of verifying a signature on an initiative or referendum petition, the Secretary of State must verify that the residence address provided by a petition signer is the same as the residence address provided on the petition signer's affidavit of voter registration. A signature is not counted as valid if: the residence addresses do not match; the petition or paper does not specify the residence address; or the required information is not contained in the petition. A signature is not invalidated because of a minor discrepancy. Address verification as part of statistical sampling is sufficient to meet the requirement of signature verification.

HB 2261.digest: Credentialed health care providers who provide health care services must wear a visible identification badge during all patient encounters. The badge must include the health care provider's name, health care credential, and the initials of any health care-related degrees that they hold. The identification badge requirement does not apply to health care providers providing custodial services or who work in nonpatient settings and do not have any direct patient contact. Any advertisement for health care services that names a health care provider must also include the type of health care credential that the health care provider holds as well as the initials and title of any health care-related degrees. A violation of the identification badge or advertisement requirements is considered unprofessional conduct. Hospitals, assisted living facilities, nursing homes, adult family homes, and ambulatory surgical facilities must provide updated badges to health care providers upon the occurrence of several specified events. An updated identification badge is required: upon hiring a new health care provider to provide health care services; upon a new identification badge photograph being required; upon the name change of a health care provider; upon a health care provider's receipt of a new health care credential or health care-related degree; when a new credentialing period begins; or on January 1, 2030. Persons are prohibited from representing themselves as either an "osteopathic physician surgeon" or a "physician surgeon" unless they: are either a licensed physician or osteopathic physician; have completed a surgical residency or fellowship approved by the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education or the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada; are certified or eligible for examination by a surgical board of the Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education or the Royal College of Physicians and Surgeons of Canada; and maintain continuing education and proficiency in their specialty. A violation of the title protection provisions for physicians and osteopathic physicians is considered unlicensed practice.

HB 2262.digest: High School Civics Instruction . Beginning with or before the 2027-28 school year, the content for the mandatory, stand-alone high school civics course must include instruction in producing a legible, repeatable, official cursive signature, and how signatures are used by election officials in election, initiative, referenda, and recall processes. Students are not required to produce a legible, repeatable, official cursive signature as a condition for earning credit for the mandatory civics course. The development of applicable curricula may be coordinated with the Office of the Secretary of State and county auditors in accordance with required community outreach plans. The signature-related instruction should include an historical overview of signatures in a civics context, including how signature practices and exclusions have limited civic participation by historically marginalized communities. Election Reporting Requirements . The statewide survey of voted ballot rejection rates produced in odd-numbered years must include the number and rates of ballots that were rejected for signature mismatch by voter age groupings. The survey must also be provided to the Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI) for inclusion in their website content pertaining to civic education. Any election reports for the state that are published annually by the Secretary of State must also include the number and rates of ballots that were rejected for signature mismatch by voter age groupings. These reports must also be provided to the OSPI for inclusion in their website content pertaining to civic education. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: In comparison to the original bill, the substitute bill: removes a requirement obligating the State Board of Education to include school district compliance with the signature-related instruction requirements in its annual monitoring of school district compliance with basic education requirements; adds that a student's signature, for purposes of the instruction requirements, may be a personalized, handwritten signature or mark that aligns with the student's primary language or culture; adds that the signature-related instruction should include an historical overview of signatures in a civics context, including how signature practices and exclusions have limited civic participation by historically marginalized communities; and adds that students are not required to produce a legible, repeatable, official cursive signature as a condition for earning credit for the mandatory high school civics course.

HB 2265.digest: Tenant Installation of Portable Cooling Devices . Under both the RLTA and the MHLTA, a landlord may not prohibit or restrict a tenant from installing a portable cooling device, except in the following circumstances: when the installation of the portable cooling device would violate building codes or state or federal law, violate the manufacturer's written safety guidelines for the portable cooling device, cause unreasonable damage to the premises or render the premises uninhabitable, cause unreasonable damage to the manufactured/mobile home or manufactured/mobile home community, or require amperage to power the portable cooling device that cannot be accommodated by the power service to the building, manufactured/mobile home community, dwelling unit, manufactured/mobile home, or circuit; when the portable cooling device would be installed in a window and: the window is a necessary egress from the dwelling unit or manufactured/mobile home; the portable cooling device would interfere with the tenant's ability to lock a window that is accessible from outside; the portable cooling device requires the excessive use of hardware that would damage or void the warranty of the window or frame, puncture the exterior wall of the building or manufactured/mobile home, or cause significant damages; the installation of the portable cooling device in the window would not allow adequate drainage; or the portable cooling device cannot be secured in a way that prevents it from falling out of the window; or when the dwelling or manufactured/mobile home already has a permanently installed and fully operational heat pump that is capable of cooling the dwelling or home. "Portable cooling device" means air conditioners and evaporative coolers. This term includes devices designed to be mounted in a window or sit on the floor, but does not include devices whose installation or use requires alteration to the dwelling unit or the manufactured/mobile home. A landlord who limits the use of portable cooling devices due to inadequate power service must prioritize allowing the use of portable cooling devices for tenants who require it to accommodate a disability. A landlord is not responsible for any interruption in electrical service that is not caused by the landlord. A landlord must include written information in the rental agreement or lease notifying a tenant of the tenant's rights, responsibilities, and restrictions related to installation and operation of a portable cooling device. A landlord is immune from liability for any claim for damages, injury, or death caused by a portable cooling device installed by a tenant. Landlord Duty to Provide Cooling . Under the RLTA, landlords must provide facilities adequate to supply cooling as reasonably required by the tenant, as well as maintain all cooling facilities and appliances supplied by the landlord in reasonably good working order. The terms "excessive heat warning" and "excessive heat watch" are updated to "extreme heat warning" and "extreme heat watch," respectively. This aligns with changes made to these terms by the NWS. Prohibition on Physical Evictions During Periods of Extreme Heat . Sheriffs are prohibited from executing writs of restitution or physically evicting tenants during periods of extreme heat. A "period of extreme heat" is defined as a period of time beginning 24 hours before the effective time of any heat-related alert announced in advance by the NWS, or beginning at the effective time of any heat

HB 2266.digest: Shelters, Transitional Housing, Emergency Housing, and Permanent Supportive Housing . Cities must allow transitional housing and permanent supportive housing in an zones within an urban growth area in which residential dwelling units or hotels are allowed. Indoor emergency shelters and indoor emergency housing must be allowed in any area within an urban growth area in which hotels are allowed. Indoor emergency shelters and indoor emergency housing must be allowed in additional zones if necessary to meet projected needs identified in the comprehensive plan. Counties planning under the Growth Management Act are subject to the same requirements in urban growth areas. Transitional housing, permanent supportive housing, indoor emergency shelters, and indoor emergency housing (STEP housing) may not be located in an area zoned for industrial use. A county or city is not required to approve a permit application for STEP housing proposed in a critical area in which no residential development is permitted, an area of natural hazards that generally prohibit residential development, or on agricultural, forest, or mineral lands of long-term commercial significance. A county or city subject to this requirement may generally not require any standards, conditions, or requirements for STEP housing that are more restrictive than those required for other types of lodging or residential development in the zone. However, the city or county may apply any objective development regulations, including form-based codes, that are not required for lodging or residential development such as density limits, dimensional standards, height restrictions, floor area ratios, setback, lot coverage, stormwater, and tree canopy and retention requirements. Similarly, the city or county may only apply the same development permit and environmental review processes to STEP housing that apply to lodging or residential development in the same zone, unless otherwise required by state law, such as shoreline regulations and building, energy, and electrical codes. If applying design review for STEP housing, only administrative design review may be required. "Administrative design review" for cities is defined as a development permit process in which an application is reviewed, approved, or denied by the planning director (or designee) based solely on objective design and development standards without a public predecision hearing, unless the review is otherwise required by state or federal law or the structure is a designated landmark or within a historic district established under a local preservation ordinance. A city may approve requests for variances from locally established design review standards. A county or city may require the sponsor or managing agency of an indoor emergency shelter or indoor emergency housing to certify in writing that it has, between the date the permit application was approved and the date the certificate of occupancy was issued: provided the name, if any, of the facility and the headquarters address of the managing entity; provided a description of any other programs operating in the building and copies of the applicable licenses and certifications held by the program; notified residents within 500 feet of the facility; conducted more than one public meeting; designated at least one point of contact authorized to make decisions and take corrective action in emergencies; provided at least one telephone number to be used in emergencies; provided documentati

HB 2267.digest: By January 1, 2029, the Department of Commerce (Department) must produce a model urban forestry ordinance and guidance on matters related to urban forestry for use by local governments. The Department must review and update the ordinance at least every 10 years in order to ensure that the options in the ordinance are effective and actionable. HB 2271.digest: PCRC 2.0 Products . New minimum PCRC requirements are established for the following products (PCRC 2.0 products): For packaging that is a rigid plastic container, the requirement is 30 percent PCRC for products manufactured after January 1, 2029. This requirement applies to packaging with a minimum volume of 2 ounces, is capable of maintaining its shape when empty, is comprised primarily of one or more plastic resins, and is not used in certain direct food contact applications. For the following rigid plastic products, the requirement is 30 percent PCRC for products manufactured after January 1, 2029: (a) buckets and pails; (b) household storage and organization containers and lids; (c) waste containers and lids other than roll carts; (d) nursery pots or trays; (e) bulk shipping or storage containers; (f) household cleaning containers; and (g) indoor and outdoor furniture. For roll carts, the requirement is 10 percent PCRC for those manufactured beginning January 1, 2029, and 30 percent PCRC for those manufactured beginning January 1, 2031. For film plastics manufactured beginning January 1, 2029, the requirement is 10 percent PCRC. Fifteen categories of container or product types are exempted from PCRC 2.0 product requirements, including packaging in direct contact with certain foods, beverages, and medicines; packaging for infant formula, medical food, and oral nutritional supplements; packaging for hazardous or flammable products; and compostable packaging. Requirements for PCRC 1.0 Products . A variety of changes are made to PCRC requirements for PCRC 1.0 products, including that: PCRC requirements are specified to apply based on the date when a PCRC 1.0 product is manufactured. Plastic beverage container PCRC requirements are specified to apply only to hermetically sealed or otherwise capped and airtight containers other than cups. The minimum size of personal household cleaning and personal care product containers subject to PCRC requirements is reduced from 8 ounces to 2 ounces. Ecology may adjust the minimum thickness of plastic trash bags to a thickness of less than 0.7 mils if a significant portion of the market redesigns to thinner bags. Producers of plastic trash bags must begin labeling the packaging containing the bags with the minimum PCRC content, beginning in 2027. Plastic trash bag producers must submit a third-party certificate of compliance with PCRC requirements to Ecology. A decision by Ecology to adjust the minimum PCRC requirement for a PCRC 1.0 product must take effect 24 months after an Ecology determination to adjust the rate, rather than applicable in the year immediately following the decision. Any exclusions from PCRC requirements for household cleaning and personal care products regulated under the federal Insecticide, Rodenticide and Fungicide Act (FIFRA) must be granted for a minimum period of four years. Provisions Applicable to Both PCRC 1.0 Products and PCRC 2.0 Products . The producer of a PCRC 1.0 product or PCRC 2.0 product is specified to be: the manufacturer, brand or trademark owner or licensee, brand owner, importer into the United States, or distributor into the state, in descending order of responsibility. De minimis producers that have an inflation-adjusted annual global gross revenue of $5 million are not subject to PCRC requirements for PCRC 1.0 products or PCRC 2.0 products, but must register and report to Ecology in the same manner as other producers. HB 2273.digest: The SBCC must adopt and amend rules relating to embodied carbon emissions reduction standards. In developing the rules, the SBCC is required to consult with appropriate state agencies, including the Department of Enterprise Services, the Department of Commerce (Commerce), the Department of Ecology, the University of Washington, an existing technical work group with relevant expertise, and other interested parties. The embodied carbon emissions reduction standards apply to all new construction, additions, and renovations of 100,000 square feet or larger of any building covered by the International Building Code. Building projects may comply with embodied carbon emissions reduction standards through one of three paths. Path One—Existing Building Reuse . Building projects that maintain at least 45 percent of an existing structure and envelope comply with the embodied carbon emissions reduction requirements. A building project that complies under this pathway may not add more than 50 percent to the total area. The SBCC is directed to adopt rules to determine how the 45 percent reuse will be calculated. Path Two—Covered Products . As an alternative to paths one and three, all building projects subject to the embodied carbon emissions reduction standards must demonstrate that the embodied carbon emissions of covered products used for the project meet established reduction requirements. The reduction is measured in terms of global warming potential for at least 90 percent of covered projects and summed up at the project level when compared to the project's summed industry average global warming potential. To achieve the reduction, building products must use project-specific as-built material quantities and product- and facility-specific EPDs to demonstrate compliance. The SBCC is directed to adopt rules defining how covered products are calculated. The SBCC must adopt rules to define covered products, how the 90 percent of covered products will be calculated, and establish how the industry average will be determined. A building's design professional of record must update material quantities and embodied carbon emissions calculations based on product- and facility-specific EPDs from procured products and attest that they are accurate and comply with project documents before substantial completion. Calculations must be verified as accurate within the industry standard of care with a letter stamped by a design professional of record. The SBCC is directed to create a template reporting form for consistent reporting on materials, including guidance on calculating compliance with reduction targets. Path Three—Whole Building Life-Cycle Assessment . As an alternative to paths one and two, a building project may demonstrate the embodied carbon emissions reductions using a whole building life-cycle assessment (WBLCA) as compared against a functionally equivalent reference building. A WBLCA is an assessment covering specified life-cycle stages of a product or system to evaluate the environmental impacts of a building, including global warming potential. The reference building must be of the same size, geographic location, function, type, and thermal performance as the proposed building. The SBCC is directed to adopt rules to require compliance with a quantification standard for building life-cycle greenhouse gas emissions. Alternatively, the SBCC may adopt rules to specify required building element metrics. The design professional of record responsible f

HB 2281.digest: Government-to-Government Consultation . General. The government-to-government consultation process between a state agency and a tribe must be mutually agreed upon. "Indian tribe" is redefined as any federally recognized Indian tribe with traditional lands and territories in Washington. Tribal Traditional Cultural Places. Before taking any agency action that may affect a tribal traditional cultural place, a state agency must comply with the consultation requirements of Executive Order 21-02. "Agency actions" are defined as projects proposed in state-funded construction or acquisition projects covered by Executive Order 21-02. "Tribal traditional cultural place" is defined as any geophysical or geographical place, area, or feature associated with the cultural practices, traditions, beliefs, lifeways, arts, crafts, or social institutions of an Indian tribe. "Traditional" is defined as those beliefs, customs, and practices of an Indian tribe that have been passed down through generations and the places associated with those beliefs, customs, and practices. Cause of Action . A state agency may not impose an undue burden or interfere with an Indian tribe's exercise of traditional cultural practices on a tribal traditional cultural place unless it is in furtherance of a compelling governmental interest and is the least restrictive means of furthering that compelling governmental interest. An Indian tribe may bring a claim in superior court for a violation of this requirement. An action against a state agency must be commenced within three years of the agency action. Burden of Proof. If the tribal traditional cultural place or practice can be disclosed, the tribe has the burden of proving that the agency action poses an undue burden on a tribal traditional cultural practice or on the management, use, or preservation of a tribal traditional cultural place. If the tribe meets this burden, the agency must then prove that the governmental interest in the state action is compelling and that the agency chose the least intrusive means for satisfying that governmental interest. If a tribe's traditional cultural tenets prohibit disclosure about a tribal traditional cultural place or practice, it is the agency's burden to prove that: it has a compelling governmental interest in pursuing the action; it is essential that the agency's compelling governmental issue be furthered as originally proposed; and none of the less intrusive alternatives identified adequately advance that compelling governmental interest. An agency may not proceed with the proposed action if it does not meet its burden of proof. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: The substitute bill redefines "agency action" to mean projects proposed in state-funded construction or acquisition projects covered by Executive Order 21-02. The substitute bill removes the reference to "contemporary" lands in the definition of "Indian tribe." The substitute bill eliminates the consultation requirements for an agency action that may affect a tribal traditional cultural place in the original bill and instead requires state agencies to comply with the consultation requirements of Executive Order 21-02 before taking any agency action that may affect a tribal traditional cultural place. The substitute bill establishes a three year statute of limitation for an action against a state agency for imposing an undue burden on interfering with an Indian tribe's exercise of traditional cultural practices on a tr

HB 2283.digest: Fully insured individual, small group, and large group health plans issued or renewed on or after January 1, 2028, must have a medical loss ratio of at least 90 percent. The Insurance Commissioner may adopt rules necessary to implement this requirement. The Insurance Commissioner may require health carriers to submit information regarding a carrier's calculation of the medical loss ratio as part of a carrier's health plan rate filings for plan years beginning on or after January 1, 2027. This information may include: (1) a carrier's reimbursement or payments to a carrier's owned or affiliated health care providers or facilities, health care benefit managers, or other entities; (2) a carrier's use of nonclaims-based payments; and (3) a carrier's payments for quality improvement, risk mitigation, and other incentive-based activities. Medical loss ratio is defined as a health carrier's incurred claims plus the carrier's expenditures for activities to improve health care quality (e.g., prevent hospital readmissions, improve patient safety, reduce medical errors, promote wellness) divided by the health carriers premium revenue (excluding federal and state taxes and licensing and regulatory fees) accounting for payments or receipts related to risk adjustment, risk corridors, or reinsurance.

Ecology is directed to convene a task force to provide policy recommendations with the goal of ensuring a net decrease in litter. Ecology may contract with an independent third-party facilitator to convene the task force. The task force must consist of representatives of 15 specified interests, including representatives of eight specified types of associations, and six specified state agencies. Ecology must submit a status update to the appropriate committees of the Legislature by January 15, 2027, and a final report consisting of the recommendations of the task force by November 15, 2027.

HB 2285.digest: An electric utility may satisfy its 2030 and 2045 CETA obligations by using electricity from certain natural gas systems operated with carbon capture and utilization, mineralization, or sequestration (CCUS) technology. The CCUS technology must comply with all local, state, and federal laws and have a capture design capacity of at least 75 percent of the baseline carbon dioxide (CO2) production of the applicable natural gas system. The method for calculating the baseline CO2 production of a natural gas system depends on the date that the gas system was originally placed in service: If the gas system was originally placed into service within a one-year period prior to the beginning of construction of the CCUS system, or the gas system had not yet been placed into service as of the beginning of construction of the CCUS system, the baseline CO2 production is the designed annual CO2 production, by mass, as determined based on an assumed 60 percent capacity factor. If the gas system was originally placed in service between one year and three years prior to the beginning of construction of the CCUS system, the baseline CO2 production is the average annual CO2 production by mass during the period between when the natural gas system was placed in service and when the CCUS construction began. If the gas system was originally placed in service more than three years prior to the beginning of construction of the CCUS system, the baseline CO2 production is the average of the three-year period with the highest annual CO2 production during the 12-year period before the beginning of construction of the CCUs system. An electric utility that has not achieved its 2030 CETA obligations is in compliance with CETA if it demonstrates that it has maximized investments in electricity from natural gas systems operated with CCUS, in addition to maximizing investments in electricity from renewable resources and non-emitting electric generation. Natural gas systems operated with CCUS are given treatment equivalent to renewable resources or non-emitting generation for other purposes under CETA, including for CEIP purposes, and for petitions by an investor-owned utility to the UTC for a declaratory order regarding the compliance of a proposed project with 2030 and 2045 CETA obligations.

HB 2291.digest: The Kratom Consumer Protection Act (Act) is established. Licensing Requirement . A kratom retailer license and a kratom processor license are established to be administered by the Liquor and Cannabis Board (LCB). No person may operate as a kratom retailer or a kratom processor in the state without being licensed; however, no person may hold both a kratom retailer license and a kratom processor license. Operating as a kratom retailer or kratom processor without being licensed is a class C felony. Applications for a license may be submitted to the LCB for approval. The application fee and annual renewal fee for either license is $1,000, and kratom retailers need to pay a license fee for each separate retail location. Age Restriction . Persons under 21 years of age are prohibited from purchasing kratom products. A person under 21 years of age who purchases, possesses, or obtains, or attempts to purchase or obtain, kratom products commits a class 3 civil infraction and is subject to four hours of community service. Licensed retailers must display appropriate signage, designed by the Department of Health, that states: "The sale of kratom products to persons under age 21 is strictly prohibited by state law." Retailers must verify the age of consumers who purchase kratom products with government-issued identification when there may be a question of a person's right to purchase. Unsecured displays open to the general public and self-service displays for kratom products are prohibited, except when a retail establishment only permits persons aged 21 and older to enter. A person who sells or gives, or permits to be sold or given, kratom in any form to an underage person is guilty of a gross misdemeanor. Prohibitions Practices . Kratom products are prohibited from being consumed in public, and a person who violates the prohibition is guilty of a class 3 civil infraction. No person may conduct a delivery sale of, ship, or transport any kratom product ordered or purchased by mail or online. A person who knowingly violates this is guilty of a class C felony, with a maximum criminal fine of $5,000 and a potential civil penalty of up to $5,000 for each violation. The Attorney General may seek recovery in civil action, along with an injunction and reasonable attorney's fees and other costs. If a court finds that a person violated this prohibition, any profits received due to the violation are to be disgorged and paid to the State General Fund. A licensee who violates this prohibition is subject to license suspension or revocation. A violation is also a per se violation of the Consumer Protection Act. Penalties and remedies are cumulative. No person may offer a tasting or free sample of kratom to the public. A violation is a misdemeanor. Labeling Requirements . Kratom products must contain a label that includes information about the processor, directions for use that include recommended serving size, and an ingredient list that includes kratom alkaloids. Kratom products must also have a label with the following: a statement that kratom is illegal for use by persons under the age of 21; a statement that recommends against the use of kratom for individuals who are pregnant or breastfeeding; a statement that kratom may be habit-forming; a recommendation to consult a health professional before use; and a statement that reads, "These statements have not been evaluated by the United States Food and Drug Administration. This product is not intended to diagnose,

HB 2296.digest: Utility Company Rental Housing Energy Investments . The Utilities and Transportation Commission (UTC) must allow an electric or natural gas company (utility company) to invest in programs that achieve energy conservation and improve the efficiency of energy end use of single-family and multifamily rental housing (rental housing energy investments), instead of requiring the owner to finance cost-effective measures. The UTC may allow the utility company to earn a return on cost-effective rental housing energy investments over a time period that: reduces the customer's energy burden and minimizes the investment's impact of the customer's bill; and provides a return on equity that incentivizes the utility to make the investment. The utility company must prioritize rental housing energy investments to reduce the energy burden of low-income customers, vulnerable populations, and customers in highly impacted communities while meeting the customer's comfort and productivity needs. Rental housing energy investments must be secured through the meter and recovered through the regular billing paid by the tenant, successor tenant, or owner of the premises. If the bill is paid by the owner, the utility company's rental housing energy investment must be recovered pursuant to a site-specific services agreement. The rental housing energy investment must be: recovered as any other energy charge until the authorized return on the investment has been fully recovered; and designated as an energy savings charge as a line-item on the customer's bill. The utility company must provide the owner sufficient information for the owner to provide to their tenant who is responsible for paying the electric or gas bill. The owner must notify a tenant at least 30 days prior to the commencement of work to install conservation measures at the premises. The notice must include a description of the work to be performed and expected benefits of the conservation measure.

HB 2297.digest: Part I . Cities are authorized to adopt preferential rates for the city B&O tax. Part II . Sales made to grocery stores located in underserved community zones are exempt from retail sales tax on security and investigative services. The exemption is in the form of a remittance and is limited to one application per quarter. Part III . A property tax exemption program for grocery stores located in underserved community zones is created. A city governing authority may, by ordinance or resolution, establish an underserved community grocery store property tax exemption program to provide property tax exemptions to preserve existing grocery stores, to incentivize the rehabilitation of existing or vacant grocery store buildings, and to incentivize the construction of new grocery store buildings in underserved communities located in a city. A county governing authority is authorized to establish the same program for grocery stores in underserved communities located in unincorporated areas of a county. Exemption . The governing authority may offer 30-year exemptions from state and local property taxes, except for property taxes levied by school districts, for existing grocery stores, rehabilitated grocery stores, and newly constructed grocery stores. Grocery stores receiving the exemption must be located in an underserved community zone designated by a county. Properties to be rehabilitated or new construction projects must meet all construction and development regulations of the city or county, and be a party to a contract with the city or county under which the applicant has agreed to the implementation of the development on terms and conditions satisfactory to the city or county. The exemption does not apply to the value of the land. Property is exempted based on the type of grocery store, and is as follows: for existing grocery stores: the value of the real property consisting of a grocery store building or a portion of a building used as a grocery store; for rehabilitated grocery stores: the value of the new construction and the value of the real property consisting of a grocery store or a portion of a building used as a grocery; and for newly constructed grocery stores: the value of the new construction consisting of a grocery store or a portion of a building used as a grocery store. At the conclusion of the exemption period, the cost of new construction and rehabilitative improvements to the property must be considered as new construction. Designation of Underserved Community Zones . The governing authority of a county may designate an underserved community zone if it determines that a contiguous group of census tracts within the city's or county's jurisdiction fulfills the following requirements. The area must meet: one or more low-income criteria and the low-access criterion; or the criterion for health disadvantaged areas and the low-access criterion; or the criterion for a low-transportation-access area. The total underserved community zone designations allowed per county are limited to 10 per urban county, five per rural county, and three per frontier county. The governing authority of a county, when designating an underserved community zone, must consider designating zones in areas with the highest disparities and where the highest number of Washingtonians will be positively affected. A city may apply to the governing authority of a county to request the creation of an underserved community zone using an application process designate

HB 2298.digest: County auditors may develop and implement voluntary fraud title protection programs with the goal of preventing land record fraud. These programs may be coordinated with the county treasurer or excise agent. A voluntary property title protection program may allow property owners the option of recording a protection instrument in order to prohibit the transfer of ownership of the property without the use of a personal identification number or other approved override process, or until a release of the fraud protection instrument is recorded. If an auditor receives an instrument that would transfer ownership or real property for which a fraud protection instrument has been recorded, the auditor can delay the recording of the document transferring ownership for up to five business days. Similarly, a county treasurer or excise agent may delay processing a real estate excise tax refund application for up to five days if the property for which the refund application is submitted is the subject of a recorded fraud protection instrument. The recording of fraud protection instruments, and documents releasing such instruments, are exempt from the covenant homeownership program assessment, the growth management planning and review fund surcharge, and the surcharge related to housing. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: The substitute bill authorizes a county treasurer or excise agent to delay processing a real estate excise tax refund application for up to five days if the property for which the refund was sought is subject to a recorded property fraud protection instrument.

HB 2320.digest: Restrictions on manufacturing various firearms and related components are modified to expressly reference the use of three-dimensional (3D) printers, computer numerical control (CNC) milling machines, and digital firearm manufacturing code. Restrictions are established regarding: (1) the sale, transfer, and distribution of digital firearm manufacturing code; and (2) manufacturing frames and receivers and unfinished frames and receivers through the use of a 3D printer, CNC milling machine, or by other means, subject to various exceptions. Restrictions on Manufacturing Undetectable Firearms, Other Firearms, and Components . No person may manufacture, including by use of a 3D printer, CNC milling machine, or other means, any machine gun, bump-fire stock, undetectable firearm, short-barreled shotgun, or short-barreled rifle; or any part designed and intended solely and exclusively for use in the same, or in converting a weapon into a machine gun, short-barreled shotgun, or short-barreled rifle; subject to various exceptions. No person may manufacture, including by use of a 3D printer, CNC milling machine, or other means, an untraceable firearm with intent to sell the untraceable firearm. A violation of these restrictions is a class C felony. Restrictions on Manufacturing Untraceable Firearms . No person may manufacture, cause to be manufactured, assemble, or cause to be assembled an untraceable firearm, including by use of a 3D printer, CNC milling machine, or other means. A violation of this restriction is a civil infraction. A second violation is a misdemeanor. A third or subsequent violation is a gross misdemeanor. No person may knowingly or recklessly allow, facilitate, aid, or abet the manufacture or assembly of an undetectable firearm or untraceable firearm, including by distribution of digital firearm manufacturing code, by certain prohibited persons. A violation of this restriction is a gross misdemeanor. Restrictions on Manufacturing a Frame or Receiver or Unfinished Frame or Receiver . No person may knowingly or recklessly manufacture a frame or receiver or an unfinished frame or receiver by use of a 3D printer, CNC milling machine, or by other means, unless that person is a federal firearms manufacturer or federal firearms dealer for the sole purpose of repairing existing firearms. A violation of this restriction is a civil infraction. A second violation is a misdemeanor. A third or subsequent violation is a gross misdemeanor. A violation involving three or more frames or receivers or unfinished frames or receivers is a gross misdemeanor. A person commits a separate violation for each frame or receiver, or unfinished frame or receiver. Restrictions on Digital Firearm Manufacturing Code . No person may sell, transfer, distribute, or offer to sell digital firearm manufacturing code for a firearm or unfinished frame or receiver to a person who is not licensed to manufacture firearms under federal law. No person may possess digital firearm manufacturing code for a firearm or unfinished frame or receiver with an intent to distribute the code to a person who is not a federal firearms dealer for the sole purpose of repairing existing firearms, or with an intent to manufacture a firearm or unfinished frame or receiver using a 3D printer or CNC milling machine. HB 2325.digest: Tourism Assessment Program . The Authority is authorized to establish a Tourism Assessment Program (TAP), subject to review by the Director of Commerce, that is designed, proposed, and governed by the Ratepayer Oversight Board (ROB), described below. The Authority is required to levy and collect a percentage of a business's gross revenue as an annual assessment. The assessments will be collected on an annual basis, after ratification by the businesses in each industry sector. The membership of the Authority's Board is modified by expanding the number of members from 13 to 17, and specifying the non-legislative membership as follows: eight members must be nominated by the ROB and must represent businesses paying the assessments; two members must represent official state destination marketing organizations; two members must represent tourism businesses subject to the assessment; and one member must represent a trade association that represents businesses that are subject to the assessment. The Authority, with review of the Director of Commerce, is required to approve an annual budget for the TAP. The Authority is required to approve or reject the budget recommended by the ROB and may not amend, replace, or independently adopt policies or provisions not submitted by the ROB. The budget is required to include: a complete and detailed financial program of the ROB, showing its revenues and expenditures; an explanation describing the administration and implementation of the ROB's programs and priorities, and identifying reasons for changes from prior expenditures or revenue items; an explanation of changes to financial policies, including an outline of the proposed policies for the ensuing fiscal period and performance indicators that demonstrate measurable progress toward the ROB's priorities; and sufficient detail to provide transparency for the ROB's actions on behalf of the industry. A regular audit of the budget is required to be conducted by the State Auditor. The Authority is required to submit an annual report to the Legislature and the Governor. The Authority is required to adopt rules and give substantial weight to the recommendations in the October 31, 2025, report titled Tourism Self-Supported Assessment Advisory Group: Report to the Legislature and the ROB's proposal. The rules do not apply to federally recognized Indian tribes, businesses, or enterprises unless the tribe or tribal member has opted to participate in the TAP. The state and its agents are immune from liability for obligations incurred by the Authority or the ROB. Liabilities and claims against the Authority or ROB are only enforceable against the assets of the Authority or ROB as if it were a corporation. The liability of the members of the Authority and ROB are several, not joint, and no member shall be liable for the default of any other member. Ratepayer Oversight Board . The Authority is required to appoint an initial 10-member ROB. The Group is required to prepare a list of nominees for the initial ROB membership. The initial ROB members must include two representatives for each of the tourism business sectors: lodging, travel services, attractions, recreation, beverage producers, full-service restaurants, and retailer locations. An ROB nominee must be an employee or officer of a business proposed to be subject to the assessment. HB 2332.digest: State and local government agencies are generally prohibited from using ALPR systems. Only certain agencies may access, operate, or use ALPR systems and associated data for specifically authorized purposes. Authorized agencies are prohibited from certain practices and must comply with the registration, reporting, and audit requirements, as well as with prescribed retention periods for ALPR data. Law Enforcement . A law enforcement agency may use an ALPR system for the purpose of comparing ALPR data with: data on any of the specified watch lists maintained by a federal or Washington agency; or license plate numbers that have been manually entered into an ALPR database upon an officer's determination that the numbers are material to an investigation of a stolen vehicle, a vehicle associated with a missing or endangered person, a vehicle registered to a person for whom there is an outstanding felony warrant, or a vehicle involved in a felony. A law enforcement agency that uses a watch list must ensure that the watch list is updated at least once every 24 hours. A positive match by an ALPR system alone does not constitute reasonable suspicion as grounds for a law enforcement officer to stop the vehicle. The officer must: develop independent reasonable suspicion for the stop; or confirm visually that the vehicle license plate matches the license plate image on the ALPR system and confirm by other means that the license plate number is on one of the specified watch lists. Parking Enforcement . An ALPR system may be used for parking or toll enforcement as follows: as a component of a photo toll system; by a parking enforcement agency for the purpose of enforcing time restrictions on the use of parking spaces; or by a parking enforcement agency for the purpose of identifying vehicles on a watch list that contains only vehicles subject to impoundment or immobilization pursuant to a local ordinance and that is updated at least once every 24 hours. Transportation Agencies . A transportation agency may use an ALPR system to provide real-time traffic information, for traffic modeling or traffic studies purposes, or to enforce commercial vehicle systems at Washington State Patrol enforcement sites and weigh stations. Prohibited Practices . It is unlawful for any agency to use an ALPR system for immigration investigation or enforcement, any protected health care services, or to track or monitor an activity protected by the state Constitution and the First Amendment to the United States Constitution.

HB 2333.digest: Funding Sources—Candidates and Elected Officials . Active Campaign Funds. The list of reimbursable direct out-of-pocket expenses is expanded to include personal security measures necessary to address dangers or threats that would not exist but for the person's status or duties as a candidate or elected official, on the condition that the personal security measure is reasonably proportional in scope to the level of danger or threat that exists. Surplus Funds. Expenses related to personal security measures necessary to address dangers or threats that would not exist but for the individual's status as a candidate or elected official are considered public office-related expenses for which surplus funds may be used to purchase personal security measures on the condition that the personal security measure is reasonably proportional in scope to the level of danger or threat that exists. Definitions. Personal security measure includes, but is not limited to: nonstructural security devices, such as security hardware, locks, alarm systems, motion detectors, security camera systems, and subscriptions for security systems; structural security devices, such as wiring, lighting, gates, doors, and fencing, so long as such devices are intended solely to provide security and not to improve the property or increase its value; security personnel and services that are bona fide, legitimate, professional, and provided by a person licensed under state law; and cybersecurity software, devices, and services, including those that remove residential addresses from existing websites, and credit monitoring and identity theft monitoring services. Limitations. Any funds authorized to be used to purchase a personal security measure, or to reimburse an individual for direct out-of-pocket expenses incurred to purchase a personal security measure, may not be used to pay the individual's spouse or registered domestic partner, child, parent, grandparent, grandchild, brother, sister, parent-in-law, brother-in-law, sister-in-law, nephew, niece, aunt, uncle, or first cousin, or the spouse of any such person, or an entity in which any such person has a personal beneficial interest. Reimbursements for expenses incurred to purchase personal security measures must be for the usual and normal charge for such goods or services. Statutory Protections Against Threats and Violence . Washington State Patrol . The Chief Clerk of the House of Representatives and the Secretary of the Senate may, upon the request of a legislator, contract with the WSP to provide security to legislators at public events that have a legislative nexus where local law enforcement is unable or unwilling to provide security. Address Confidentiality Program. An elected official and any person residing with the elected official may be admitted into to the ACP by submitting an application to the Office of the Secretary of the State that includes: a designation of the Secretary as the agent authorized to receive legal service of process and mail on behalf of the applicant ; the residential address and phone number where the applicant can be contacted by the Secretary; and the signature of the applicant and date on which the application was signed. A person who knowingly provides false or incorrect information on an application or falsely attests in an application that disclosure of the person's address would endanger the safety of any elected official is guilty of offering a false or forged instrument to be filed,

HB 2334.digest: Rounding of In-Person Cash Transactions . The total price or change due of any in-person cash transaction may be rounded to the nearest 5 cent increment as follows: If the final digit of a cash transaction ends in 1 cent, 2 cents, 6 cents, or 7 cents, the final digit may be rounded down to the nearest amount divisible by 5 cents. If the final digit of a cash transaction ends in 3 cents, 4 cents, 8 cents, or 9 cents, the final digit may be rounded up to the nearest amount divisible by 5 cents. If the final digit of a cash transaction ends in 0 cents or 5 cents, the final digit may not be rounded up or down. Transactions made by another form of payment, including credit and debit cards, may not be rounded. The total price of any transaction, without any rounding adjustment, may be paid by the customer at the customer's option if the customer has the exact legal tender to pay the total price. Mixed-Tender Transactions . For mixed-tender transactions, rounding applies only to the portion of the transaction paid in cash, and must not alter or affect the exact amounts authorized, cleared, or settled through any noncash payment system. Rounding by Agencies . State and local agencies may round in-person cash transactions as authorized when pennies are not available, but must remit to the state any applicable tax, fee, or charge. Tax Obligations . Rounding applies solely to the payment amount tendered and does not alter the sales price, or the amount of tax owed or collected. Any person selling goods or services must calculate and remit all taxes and fees imposed by state or municipal taxing authorities based on the sales price before rounding. The state business and occupation tax does not apply to amounts received from rounding up as authorized, nor is any deduction allowed for rounding down as authorized. The state sales and use tax must be calculated on the selling price of goods, services, or other products subject to such tax without regard to any rounding. The amount of tax due may not be rounded. Preemption and Liability . Rounding as authorized: (1) preempts any inconsistent local ordinance, regulation, or rule; (2) is not actionable under the Consumer Protection Act; and (3) does not violate any state or municipal requirement, law, regulation, or standard. Defined Terms . "Legal tender" means all coins and currencies of the United States. "Total price" means the final amount due and payable by the buyer for the purchase of any good, service, or other product, or combination thereof, after all applicable taxes and fees are applied, as well as any discounts or other adjustments that are made by the seller. "Transaction" means the entire purchase by a buyer from a seller for all goods, services, and other products, at that date and time as is shown on an invoice or receipt. A transaction may include one item or multiple items.
HB 2334.digest_source: WA Substitute House Bill Report (Summary of Bill)
HB 2334.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to adjusting the price of a cash transaction to eliminate the need for pennies;
HB 2334.title: Cash transactions/pennies

HB 2343.digest: Effective immediately upon the bill taking effect, the Department of Fish and Wildlife must obtain a water discharge permit from Ecology when operating any publicly owned facilities at which wildlife or other animals are raised in numbers and circumstances that would otherwise qualify the facility as a CAFO. Ecology must begin applying and enforcing CAFO general permit or individual permit requirements applicable to publicly owned or operated facilities that raise animals in numbers and circumstances that would qualify the facility as a CAFO. Ecology must treat a facility with more than 5000 game birds as a large CAFO subject to the most protective standards for water quality that apply to any category of CAFO. Permits issued to publicly owned facilities must include: a manure prevention plan, production area runoff controls, land application limits, and protocols for the management of dead animals, or else alternative measures required by Ecology under an updated CAFO permit that achieve equal or better outcomes; a prohibition on discharges that cause or contribute to violations of water quality standards; protocols and procedures for use of Ecology's enforcement authority; and monitoring, recordkeeping, and reporting requirements. When the agency with jurisdiction makes a referral to the applicable county prosecuting attorney and the Attorney General to notify them about the release of a person who may meet the criteria of a sexually violent predator (SVP), the agency with jurisdiction must also concurrently provide notice of the person's anticipated release date to the: sheriff of the applicable county; senator and each representative of the applicable legislative district; administrator or manager of the applicable county; and applicable chair of the board of county commissioners or county council. Notice of Conditional Release, Change of Address, Unconditional Discharge, or Escape . The list of persons that the Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) must send written notice to before an SVP's conditional release, change of address while on conditional release, or unconditional discharge, or if the SVP escapes, is expanded to include the: executive authority of the political subdivision in which the person will reside or in which placement will be made under a less restrictive alternative (LRA); senator and each representative of the legislative district in which the person will reside or in which placement will be made under an LRA; administrator or manager of the political subdivision in which the person will reside or in which placement will be made under an LRA; chair of the city council of the city, if any, in which the person will reside or in which placement will be made under an LRA; and chair of the board of county commissioners or county council, whichever is applicable, in which the person will reside or in which placement will be made under an LRA. If the court orders an SVP's conditional release or unconditional discharge, the DSHS must send written notice to all persons who are statutorily entitled to notice of an SVP's conditional release, change of address, unconditional discharge, or escape, no later than seven calendar days after the order is filed.

HB 2354.digest: A common interest community qualifies for the small community exemption if the community's amended declaration—and not just the original declaration—contains the requisite language regarding maximum assessments. Small common interest communities that consist only of middle housing are exempt from most WUCIOA provisions. Specifically, if a plat or miscellaneous community consists of no more than six middle housing units and the average annual assessment of all middle housing units does not exceed $1,000, the community is subject only to the following provisions of the WUCIOA: the requirement of a separate title for each unit as a separate parcel of real estate and a separate tax assessment based on the value of that unit together with its interest in the common elements; the prohibition of discriminatory application of building, fire, health, or safety codes and regulations by local governments against the community property based only on the fact that the property is owned as a common interest community; and general provisions that apply when a unit in a common interest community is taken or partially taken by eminent domain. All middle housing common interest communities are exempt from the requirement to prepare and annually update a reserve study if a community does not, and will not in the future, require the construction, operation, and maintenance of any reserve component to manage wastewater and protect health and safety, as well as ground and service waters. The governing documents of a common interest community may not vary from the WUCIOA on the subject of financial responsibility for electric vehicle charging stations and heat pumps. Only the owner of the charging station or heat pump exclusively serving the owner's unit bears that financial responsibility. The threshold that triggers the requirement for an association to be annually audited by a certified public accountant and that allows unit owners to waive the annual audit is increased from $50,000 to $100,000.

The term domestic worker includes any employee or independent contractor working in a private residence for four or more hours in a month as a nanny, child care provider, home care worker, personal care provider, housekeeper or cleaner, cook, gardener, or household manager, subject to certain exceptions. The exceptions include: a person performing casual labor in or about a private residence, unless the work is performed in the course of the hiring entity's trade, business, or profession; a person performing babysitting on a irregular and uncertain basis that is incidental in nature and duration; a person performing pet sitting, dog walking, or house sitting who is not also performing other domestic service work; an individual provider, or any provider employed by a home care agency if the home care agency receives certain state funds; or a person in a family relationship with, or who is a family member of, the hiring entity. Hiring entity means any person, group, or entity that provides payment to a domestic worker for the domestic worker's work or services or acts directly or indirectly in the interest of an employer in relation to an employee.

HB 2360.digest: School Use of Albuterol . Beginning with the 2027-28 school year, school districts, charter schools, state-tribal education compact schools, and private schools may maintain a supply of albuterol aerosol, powder, or solution for use in an inhaler or nebulizer (school-supplied albuterol) in a designated location on school property. School-supplied albuterol may be acquired from donation sources, but must be accompanied by a prescription. School-supplied albuterol prescriptions must be accompanied by a standing order authorizing its administration for the management of respiratory symptoms, including breathing difficulties caused by conditions such as asthma. School-supplied albuterol must be accessed and administered in accordance with the uniform procedure for the management of a student's respiratory symptoms as follows: If the student has a prescription for albuterol on file, a school nurse or designated trained school personnel may administer school-supplied albuterol. If the student does not possess albuterol or have a prescription for albuterol on file, only a school nurse may administer school-supplied albuterol. Albuterol may be maintained, accessed, and administered on public and private school property, including the school building and playground, on a school bus, and during field trips or sanctioned excursions away from school property. A school nurse or designated trained school personnel may transport and carry a reasonable quantity of school-supplied albuterol on field trips or excursions. A school must immediately notify a student’s parent or guardian when a student is administered school-supplied albuterol or a student self-administers albuterol and the school has knowledge of this self-administration. Uniform Procedure . By January 1, 2027, the Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction and the Department of Health must include, within the uniform policy addressing school staff training requirements, a uniform procedure governing when school nurses and designated trained school personnel access and administer school-supplied albuterol. If a school district elects to maintain school-supplied albuterol, it must incorporate the uniform procedure into its policies governing asthma rescue procedures for students. Employee Opt-Out . A non-nurse employee who has not agreed in writing to include the management of albuterol as a specific part of the employee's job description may file with the school district, charter school, or state-tribal education compact school a written letter of refusal declining to manage albuterol. The letter of refusal may not serve as grounds for discharge or other adverse action affecting the employee's contract status. "Management of albuterol" means the storage, maintenance, access, administration, documentation, and transportation of albuterol in accordance with a standing order and applicable written policies of the school district, charter school, or state-tribal education compact school. Liability Protections . If a student is injured or harmed due to the administration of albuterol that was lawfully prescribed and dispensed, a licensed health professional may not be held responsible for the injury unless the prescription was issued with a conscious disregard for safety. A school employee or contractor who administers albuterol in substantial compliance with a lawful albuterol prescription or standing order and written school policies is subject to limited civil and criminal liability.
HB 2360.digest_source: WA Substitute House Bill Report (Summary of Bill)
HB 2360.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to expanding access to albuterol in public and private schools;

HB 2361.digest: The maximum principal amount of any small loan, or the outstanding principal balances of all small loans made by all check casher or seller licensees to a single borrower at any one time, is increased. The $700 limit is changed to $1,200, adjusted biennially for inflation based upon changes in the Consumer Price Index (CPI). Accordingly, the maximum principal amount of any small loan, or the outstanding principal balances of all small loans made by all licensees to a single borrower at any one time, may not exceed $1,200, adjusted for inflation based upon changes in the CPI, or 30 percent of the borrower's gross monthly income, whichever is lower. Beginning January 1, 2027, and biennially thereafter, the DFI must calculate the inflation-adjusted maximum principal amount of any small loan allowed under the law, by calculating to the nearest cent using the CPI. The DFI must publish the information in the Washington State Register. For the purposes of the bill, the relevant CPI is the CPI for all urban consumers, all items, for the Seattle area as calculated by the United States Bureau of Labor Statistics or its successor agency. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: As compared to the original bill, the substitute bill: requires the inflation-adjustment to the maximum principal amount of any small loan to be biennially instead of annually; requires the DFI to publish the inflation-adjusted maximum principal amount of any small loan in the Washington State Register, instead of on the DFI's website and in a press release; removes a reference to the DFI calculating the inflation-adjusted maximum outstanding principal balances of all small loans made by all licensees to a single borrower at any one time; and changes a reference to the DFI determining, instead of calculating, the inflation-adjusted maximum principal amount of any small loan allowed under the law.

HB 2362.digest: Impaired Driving Offenses . The breath or blood alcohol concentration limit of 0.08 percent or higher is reduced to 0.05 percent or higher for the offenses of Driving While Under the Influence and Actual Physical Control of a Motor Vehicle While Under the Influence, and for the unlawful behaviors of unlawful operation of a vessel in a reckless manner and reckless or impaired driving under the Washington Code of Military Justice. Blood and Breath Tests . An alcohol concentration of less than 0.08 is reduced to 0.05 as evidence that may be considered in determining whether the person was under the influence of intoxicating liquor. The liquid simulator solution external standard or dry gas external standard result is reduced to 0.045 to 0.055 inclusive. Driver's License Suspension . The alcohol concentration of 0.08 is reduced to 0.05 for the license sanctions and disqualifications imposed by the DOL and suspension, revocation, or denial of a driver's license, permit, or privilege following a breath test for purposes of the officer's warning, written notice after arrest, sworn report, and scope of the hearing. Criminal Penalty Probation Conditions . The alcohol concentration limit of 0.08 or more is reduced to 0.05 or more for the probation conditions imposed by a court. Unlawful Sale and Purchase of Liquor . The reduction in the breath or blood alcohol concentration from 0.08 to 0.05 does not change civil law for purposes of civil liability of a licensed commercial or quasi-commercial vendor. Public Information Campaign . The Washington Traffic Safety Commission (Commission) is required to develop and implement a public information campaign related to the reduction in the breath or blood alcohol concentration from 0.08 to 0.05. The Commission is required to ensure media coverage statewide, advertise in multiple issues in each county's largest newspaper, provide content in the top nine non-English languages, consider equity outcomes on overburdened communities, and collaborate with the hospitality industry to educate drivers by developing at least 10 percent of the advertisements with the industry. Washington State Institute for Public Policy Evaluation . The Washington State Institute for Public Policy is required to evaluate the impacts of the reduction in the breath or blood alcohol concentration from 0.08 to 0.05 and submit a report by March 1, 2028. The evaluation is required to include the impact of the reduction on serious and fatal traffic crashes, arrests and adjudications for Driving Under the Influence offenses, equity outcomes on overburdened communities, and business effects on the hospitality industry, breweries, wineries, and distilleries.
HB 2362.digest_source: WA House Bill Report (Summary of Bill)
HB 2362.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to impaired driving;
HB 2362.title: Impaired driving

HB 2364.digest: The Legislative-Executive WorkFirst Poverty Reduction Oversight Task Force is renamed the Legislative-Executive Economic Justice and Well-Being Task Force (Task Force). The number of voting members of the Task Force are expanded from 8 to 11 to add the following state agencies: the Department of Revenue; the Health Care Authority; and the Workforce Training and Education Coordinating Board. The Task Force cochairs must be selected from the voting members and serve two-year terms. The Task Force representatives from the Governor's Offices of Equity, Indian Affairs, and Financial Management are identified as nonvoting members. The duties of the Task Force are modified to specify that the Task Force: oversees the budget and performance of the WorkFirst program; determines outcome and accountability measures for the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty; collaborates with the advisory council to monitor the strategies and recommendations in the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty; seeks input for poverty reduction to encourage the development of cross-sector and innovative approaches to poverty reduction; analyzes data with a primary focus on the strategies and recommendations of the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty; and collaborates with and seeks advice from the Washington Economic Justice Alliance in supporting the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty. Economic Justice and Well-Being Advisory Council . The Intergenerational Poverty Advisory Committee is renamed the Economic Justice and Well-Being Advisory Council (Council). The Secretary of the Department of Social and Health Services (DSHS) is authorized to appoint members to the Council as appropriate (in addition to the current members). The required membership of the Council is modified to: include organizations that address poverty, education, or early childhood education grants that may include faith-based organizations, but is not limited to faith-based organizations; include individuals impacted by poverty; remove a subject matter expert in infant mental health; remove a representative from the Department of Children, Youth, and Families and the DSHS; and add entities representing the workforce system and postsecondary education systems. The duties of the Council are modified to require that it monitor the strategies and recommendations outlined in the 10-year plan to dismantle poverty and recommend to the Task Force priorities and policy options that the Task Force should consider proposing to the Governor and the Legislature to effectively reduce poverty and promote and encourage self-sufficiency.
