HB 2573.digest: Notice of Closure . A supermarket, full service grocery store, or pharmacy (grocery store) that was relied upon by a jurisdiction planning under the GMA to designate an area for affordable or senior housing, housing for disabled persons, health services, increased density and transit, or infrastructure investments must provide at least six months' notice of reduced service, closure, or proposed closure or sale. A grocery store located in an overburdened community must provide at least one year's notice of closure, proposed closure or sale, or significant change in operation that may interrupt access to groceries or prescriptions or significantly affect the employment of residents of the overburdened community. The notice must be provided to the city in which the grocery store is located, any other cities or unincorporated areas of a county that comprises the affected overburdened community, and the Department of Commerce. Notice must also be included in land use permits and posed to the public. A city entitled to notice and the Washington Attorney General's Office may file an action in superior court to enjoin a closure, sale, or significant change in operation which violates the notice requirement. Zoning Tools . Cities and counties are authorized to use zoning tools and comprehensive plan updates to improve the likelihood that properties used for and relied upon for grocery services will be returned to use for grocery services. Cities and counties may designate commercial or mixed-use properties to be zoned to require one or more ongoing uses as a grocery store or to include another use that promotes public health in an overburdened community. Growth Management Act . In its next comprehensive plan update, a city or county may include designation of properties as areas of mixed commercial and residential use within one-half mile of major transit, or that otherwise are identified in the comprehensive plan as supporting multifamily housing, for uses to include a grocery store. A city may take other authorized actions including increasing the floor area ratio or density limits if development will include an enforceable covenant and permit requirement for a grocery store or other use that promotes public health for at least 25 years. A health and food access goal is added to the GMA goals. The goal aims to improve the health outcomes of people living in overburdened communities and federally recognized Indian country through access to health food, medicine, and health services. A new mandatory healthy communities element is added to the GMA. The element must include policies to improve health outcomes for residents of overburdened communities and members of federally recognized Indian tribes living in designated reservations or Indian country. Specified policies must be included. Excise Tax . Cities and counties are authorized to impose an excise tax on the owner of a property zoned for and which previously housed a grocery store whose presence was a significant factor in the city or county authorizing increased housing density, affordable housing, housing for seniors or persons with disabilities, or investment in transit, transportation, or infrastructure plans under the GMA. In adopting an excise tax, a city or county must include in its ordinance other purposes that a property may serve to reduce or eliminate the excise tax, and the extent and time period for which the city or county will reduce the tax. The excise tax may be up to $500

HB 2574.digest: Procedures are set forth for when a county auditor receives an official copy of a death certificate for a deceased candidate for a nonpartisan elective office of a city, town, or special purpose district. If a primary election is conducted for the office, and general election ballots have not been ordered, the candidate who received the third greatest number of votes in the primary election qualifies as a candidate for the general election, and their name is printed on the ballot in lieu of the deceased candidate's name. If ballots for the general election have already been ordered, votes cast for the deceased candidate are not counted. If a primary election is not conducted for the office, and general election ballots have not been ordered, the name of the deceased candidate is removed from the ballot. If ballots for the general election have already been ordered, votes for the deceased candidate are not counted. If the deceased candidate is the only candidate to have filed for the office during a regular or special filing period for the office, a void in candidacy for the office exists.

HB 2575.digest: Energy Independence Act Reporting . Qualifying utilities must submit their EIA reports to Commerce biennially, rather than annually. Qualifying utilities must report on the type and amount of RECs that were retired, rather than acquired. The reporting language is modified to clarify that instead of reporting on progress in the preceding year in meeting the targets, qualifying utilities must report on compliance in meeting the targets. Electric utilities are encouraged to use any savings from these decreased reporting requirements for low-income energy assistance. State Energy Strategy Implementation Report . The State Energy Strategy implementation report is due by December 1, 2024, and then by four years after Commerce completes its review of the State Energy Strategy. Reporting Utility Disconnections on Heat-Related Alert Days. The requirement that electric and water utilities report on the total number of disconnections that occurred on each day for which the National Weather Service issued or announced that it intended to issue a heat-related alert is eliminated. Electric utilities are encouraged to use any savings from these removed reporting requirements for low-income energy assistance. Adequacy of the State's Electricity Supply Biennial Report . The requirement for Commerce to biennially report on the adequacy of the state's electricity supply is eliminated.

HB 2577.digest: Required Timeframes for Department of Health Inspections of Acute Care Hospitals . The Department of Health (DOH) is required to inspect acute care hospitals at least every 18 months, rather than at least every 18 months on average. During a federal, state, or local emergency, the DOH may pause unannounced inspections if it determines that conducting such inspections is not in the best interest of public health. During these periods, the DOH must still investigate in response to complaints related to patient well-being. Inspections by a Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Accrediting Organization . An inspection by the DOH or a DOH-approved accrediting organization for CMS certification may be deemed equivalent to a DOH inspection if the DOH determines that the standards are substantially equivalent and the hospital provides evidence to the DOH of certification based on the inspection. Such an inspection may fulfill the requirement for DOH inspection once every 36 months. Fire Safety Inspections by the Director of Fire Protection . The Director of Fire Protection (Director) must inspect acute care hospitals at least every 18 months. If a substantially equivalent inspection is made by a CMS accrediting organization, that inspection may fulfill the requirement once every 36 months. The Director may reinspect a hospital applying for licensure, if the hospital's noncompliance with licensing standards constituted immediate jeopardy or a condition-level violation not substantially meeting licensing requirements.

HB 2578.digest: Four new commissioner positions and four alternate commissioner positions are added to the Fish and Wildlife Commission (Commission) representing federally recognized tribes whose traditional lands and territories included parts of Washington (federally recognized tribes), bringing the total number of commissioners from nine to 13, with four alternates. The quorum for the Commission to transact business and call special meetings is updated from five members to seven members. In making all appointments to the Commission, the Governor must continue to seek a balance reflecting all aspects of fish and wildlife, adding representation recommended by organized groups representing federally recognized tribes to the other entities that currently must be considered. The four new commissioners must be elected as Chair or to an equivalent executive office of a federally recognized tribe. The four alternates must be elected to a tribal council or to an equivalent legislative office of a federally recognized tribe. Two of the commissioners and two of the alternates must be from tribes located east of the Cascades, and two must be located west of the Cascades. The requirements that Commissioners not hold another elected or appointed office, be registered voters in Washington, and have general knowledge of the habitats and distribution of fish and wildlife are maintained for the current nine commission positions, but are not extended to the commissioner and alternate positions representing federally recognized tribes. Each of the commissioners and alternates representing federally recognized tribes serve staggered four-year terms, and are appointed by the Governor in January of each odd-numbered year, with the advice and consent of the Senate. While serving in their role as commissioner or alternate, each member must represent the interests of all federally recognized tribes. If a commissioner position representing federally recognized tribes is vacant, an alternate will serve in their place until the Governor appoints a new Tribal Chair to the position. If a commissioner or alternate position is vacant for any reason, the Governor must appoint a qualifying individual within 60 days. If a commissioner or alternate is no longer elected to their position as chair or councilmember of a tribe, their position is considered vacant.

HB 2579.digest: Commerce is required to establish a public media broadcaster program and a digital equity program to award funds to ensure access to the internet and noncommercial media. Commerce must seek gifts, grants, and nonstate contributions to fund the programs. Public Media Broadcaster Program . Commerce is required to award funds annually to ensure that every Washingtonian has access to noncommercial media that informs, educates, and connects Washington communities. Commerce must determine eligibility criteria for the program and must prioritize: community, public radio, or television organizations based in the state; noncommercial, nonreligious, and not-for-profit organizations; broadcasters that do not include a paywall for core program services; organizations that have provided service in the state for a minimum of seven years prior to the award; organizations that adhere to professional editorial standards; organizations whose service includes public safety, emergency broadcasting, public service announcements, access to the arts, community event promotion, and not-for-profit partnerships; organizations that make music accessible to everyone, build audiences for the arts by promoting events happening in the community, and provide a platform for artists to reach their audience and build careers; organizations whose service includes community activation, free community events calendaring, educational impacts, partnership with public schools, and services for young adults after high school graduation, including but not limited to mentoring, internships, or fellowships; demonstrated economic impact; and operations including public transparency and reporting, including but not limited to annual service and impact reports or audits. Commerce must identify criteria to prioritize the awards. The criteria must include: The relative scale and community impact must be included criteria. Eighty-five percent of the funding awards must be provided to broadcasters that have a budget in excess of $1 million. An entity may receive an award of up to eight percent of its annual operating expenses or $1.5 million, whichever is greater. Fifteen percent of the funding awards must be provided to broadcasters who have a budget of less than $1 million and serve rural or frontier counties or urban counties with a hyper-local audience. These awards may be used for annual operations or projects, and must be a minimum of $5,000 and no more than eight percent of the broadcaster's annual operating expenses. All awards must be spent within the state. Digital Equity Program . The digital equity program must provide space for trainings, computer labs, studios, pods, booths, and mobile recording and broadcast equipment. Commerce must determine eligibility criteria for the program and must prioritize: community anchor institutions such as a school, library, health clinic, health center, hospital or other medical provider, public safety entity, institution of higher education, public housing organization, or community support organization that facilitate greater use of broadband service by underserved populations; accountable communities of health, public access, education, and government television stations; workforce development councils; Washington Sta

HB 2584.digest: A sales and use tax exemption is established for the sale of qualifying farm equipment to an eligible farmer. This exemption expires on October 1, 2036. Certificate of Exemption . To obtain this exemption, the buyer must provide the seller with an exemption certificate as prescribed by the Department of Revenue (DOR). Buyers must keep records to verify eligibility for the exemption. Instead of an exemption certificate, a seller may record data as allowed under the SSUTA. The seller must retain a copy of the certificate or recorded data. Qualifying Farm Equipment . To qualify for this exemption, the farm equipment must have been acquired by an eligible farmer at a sales price of $10,000 or more. "Farm equipment" includes, but is not limited to, tractors, trailers, combines, tillage implements, balers, and other equipment, including attachments and accessories that are used in the planting, cultivating, irrigation, harvesting, and marketing of agricultural, horticultural, or livestock products, but does not include motor vehicles designed or intended for use upon public roadways or motorcycles. Eligible Farmers . To qualify for this exemption, either the gross sales or harvested value, or both, of agricultural products and bee pollination services of the eligible farmer, in combination with all affiliates of the eligible farmer, may not exceed the farm income threshold. An eligible farmer may not claim this exemption more than once, in total, each calendar year. "Eligible farmer" means a farmer who meets specified statutory requirements, including gross sales, harvested value, or estimated value of at least $10,000 in the immediately preceding tax year, or a farmer who did not engage in farming in the immediately preceding tax year because they are new to farming or newly returned to farming. "Farmer" means any person engaged in the business of growing, raising, or producing, upon the person's own lands or upon the lands in which the person has a present right of possession, any agricultural product to be sold, and the growing, raising, or producing of honey bee products for sale, or providing bee pollination services, by an eligible apiarist. "Farmer" does not include a person growing, raising, or producing such products for the person's own consumption; a person selling any animal or animal substance in connection with the person's business of operating a stockyard or a slaughter or packing house; or a person in respect to the business of taking, cultivating, or raising timber. "Farm income threshold" means $2 million in either gross sales or harvested value, or both, of agricultural products and bee pollination services in the preceding tax year. By December 2031, the DOR must adjust the farm income threshold based on the consumer price index as specified in the act. Tax Preference Performance Statement . The Legislature categorizes the tax preference in this act as one intended to provide tax relief for certain businesses or individuals. By January 1, 2035, the JLARC must evaluate the impact of these exemptions and changes in the number of small and medium-sized agricultural producers located in the State of Washington.

HB 2585.digest: The Washington False Claims Act (Act) is established. The Attorney General must diligently investigate violations of the Act. Civil Liability. Civil liability is established for the following activities involving claims for payment or approval presented to the state: knowingly presenting a false or fraudulent claim; knowingly using false records or statements material to a false or fraudulent claim; knowingly failing to return money or property to the state; intending to defraud the state through a certification of receipt of property; knowingly purchasing public property from a state employee who is not authorized to lawfully sell the property; knowingly making or using false records material to, or concealing or improperly avoiding, an obligation to pay money to the state; or conspiring to commit a violation of the Act. A claim does not include claims for payment under the state Medicaid program or requests for money or property that the state has paid to an individual as compensation for employment or as an income subsidy with no restrictions on that individual's use of the money or property. Liability for presenting such a claim includes a civil penalty of not less than the greater of $14,308 or the minimum inflation-adjusted penalty amount imposed as provided by federal law and not more than the greater of $28,619 or the maximum inflation-adjusted penalty amount imposed under federal law, plus three times the amount of damages incurred by the state. The court may reduce the damage award to double damages if the person making the claim cooperates with the Attorney General's investigation. Qui Tam Actions. Qui tam actions are authorized, allowing a private citizen, known as a "qui tam relator," to bring a civil action in the name of the state for violations of the Act. Prior to commencing the action, the qui tam relator must serve the Attorney General with a copy of the complaint and all material evidence regarding the claim. The action must be filed in camera and remain under seal for at least 60 days, with extensions allowed. The Attorney General has at least 60 days following the receipt of the complaint and the evidence to decide whether or not to intervene in the action. State Intervention. If the Attorney General intervenes in the action, the Attorney General has the primary responsibility for prosecuting the action. The relator continues as a party but the court may impose restrictions on the relator's participation in the case. The state may seek to dismiss or settle the action over the objections of the qui tam relator. The relator is entitled to notice and an opportunity to contest the motion. The court may allow a settlement over the objections of the relator if the settlement is fair, adequate, and reasonable. If the state does not intervene, the relator may proceed with the action. The state is entitled to receive copies of all pleadings and deposition transcripts in the action, and upon a showing of good cause, may intervene in the action at a later date. Proceeds of Qui Tam Action. A relator is entitled to share in the proceeds of any judgment or settlement obtained in the action. In an action conducted by the state, the relator is entitled to receive at least 15 percent but not more than 25 percent of the proceeds, depending upon the relator's contribution to the prosecution of the action, plus costs and reasonable attorneys' fees and expenses. The award to the relator is limited to no more than 10 percent of the proc

HB 2588.digest: A county that forms a ferry district must include the whole of the county within the district. Promptly after the formation of a ferry district, if the county does not already have a ferry advisory committee, the county legislative authority must appoint a five-member County Ferry District Advisory Committee. The members must be residents of the county. At least three of the members must be frequent users of the ferry system, while the other two members must represent other areas of the county. County legislative authorities are encouraged to include at least one member of a federally recognized Indian tribe on the committee. The initial appointments must be made in two groups, with one group appointed for two years and the other group appointed for four years. Thereafter, all members are appointed for four year terms. If the county is transitioning from a county ferry system to a ferry district system, and the county had an advisory committee for the ferry system, then the members of the existing committee must be appointed as the County Ferry District Advisory Committee. Members of an advisory committee must serve without fee or compensation. A ferry district's authority to operate or take other actions related to ferries, including powers related to the use of tax revenue and bond financing, is not limited to activities involving solely passenger-only ferries, but extends to ferries in general. Ferry districts created after June 10, 2026, outside of King County may not impose a property tax levy to support the district's activities at a rate greater than 10 cents per $1,000 of assessed value unless voters within the ferry district first approve the levy at a general or special election. The prohibition on operating a ferry crossing or bridge within 10 miles of a ferry crossing or toll bridge operated by the WSDOT does not apply to the operation of ferry service by a ferry district.

HB 2589.digest: A person or organization is prohibited from using an institution of higher education's campus to camp except under certain approved circumstances. An individual or organization that wishes to establish such an encampment must notify the institution 21 days prior to the establishment of the encampment. Only registered student organizations or recognized bargaining units in good standing may request authorization. An institution may authorize or deny the encampment based on the time, place, or manner of the encampment in a content-neutral process to prevent the disruption to education and other institutional activities. Any permitted encampment must serve an academic purpose. If an individual violates the institution's policies on encampments, a representative from the institution is directed to take specified action to dismantle and remove the encampment, including taking disciplinary action against the student or organization. A law enforcement agency, peace officer, or institutional campus security may remove an encampment and any individual or organization from the campus who has violated the prohibition on encampments and refuses to comply with the direction to leave. An individual is liable for all damages caused by their unauthorized encampment.

HB 2593.digest: Minimum Balances for General Funds . Each school district with 2,000 or more average annual full-time equivalent (FTE) students must have a general fund year ending balance of no less than 6 percent of their prior year's state apportionment. For other school districts, their general fund year ending balance must be no less than 8 percent of their prior year's state apportionment. The required minimum amounts—or fund balance thresholds—must be calculated by Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI) for each school district for review and adoption by its board of directors. Formal Financial Monitoring . Beginning in the 2027-28 school year, the OSPI must place school districts with general fund balances that are below required minimums at the end of the year on formal financial monitoring. School districts placed under formal financial monitoring, beginning in the 2028-29 school year, must submit monthly financial data to the OSPI. The data must include the following information for each fund of the school district: monthly expenditures; monthly revenue; end-of-month cash balance; interfund loan activity; and any other debt or borrowing transactions. For each school district placed under formal financial monitoring, the OSPI must: provide technical assistance to support the school district and avoid the imposition of binding conditions; and specify whether the school district has failed to meet the minimum general fund balance threshold in the district's financial health indicators. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: In comparison to the original bill, the substitute bill: removes provisions requiring school districts to implement minimum general fund balance requirements by the 2030-31 school year, and instead requires the Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction (OSPI), beginning in the 2027-28 school year, to place school districts with general fund balances that are below required minimum amounts at the end of the year on formal financial monitoring; removes provisions establishing maximum allowable amounts for general fund balances; removes provisions establishing allowable uses of restricted fund balance resources, including requirements for resolutions by the school district's board of directors and fund repayment plans approved by the OSPI; requires school districts that have been placed under formal financial monitoring to meet specified monthly financial reporting requirements; removes provisions authorizing the OSPI to withhold monthly apportionment payments if a school district under formal financial monitoring fails to submit required monthly financial data within 45 days of the end of a reporting month; requires the OSPI to provide technical assistance to each school district placed under formal financial monitoring to support the school district and avoid the imposition of binding conditions, and to specify in the school district's financial health indicators whether a school district has failed to meet minimum general fund balance requirements; and makes nonsubstantive technical and grammar edits, such as changing "2,000 average annual full-time equivalent students or greater" to "2,000 or more average annual full-time equivalent students," and permitting agency rules to be adopted by the "Office of" the Superintendent of Public Instruction.

HB 2597.digest: Washington Civil Actions . A person who is deprived of any rights, privileges, or immunities secured by the United States Constitution during civil immigration enforcement by any person acting under color of any law, statute, ordinance, regulation, custom, or usage may bring an action at law, suit in equity, or other proper proceeding. Recovery of Attorneys' Fees . A court may award reasonable attorneys' fees, including expert fees, to a prevailing plaintiff. Government Immunity . Defendants are provided with the defense of absolute or qualified immunity to the same extent as a person sued under a section 1983 action under like circumstances. Any defense of sovereign immunity otherwise available to a party is not waived or abrogated. Statute of Limitations . A civil action brought against a person who violates the United States Constitution while participating in civil immigration enforcement must be commenced within two years after the cause of action accrues. Severability . Severability clauses are included for any provision of the act that is held invalid or conflicts with federal requirements that are a condition to the allocation of federal funds to the state.

HB 2599.digest: Licensed Professional Use of Artificial Intelligence . A licensed professional, defined to include certain licensees that provide therapy or psychotherapy services, may not use artificial intelligence (AI) in such a way that allows it to do any of the following: make independent therapeutic decisions; directly interact with clients in any form of therapeutic communication; generate therapeutic recommendations or treatment plans without review and approval by the licensed professional; or detect emotions or mental states of clients. A licensed professional may not use AI to assist in providing supplementary support in therapy or psychotherapy where the client's therapeutic session is recorded or transcribed unless: (i) the patient or the patient's representative is informed that AI will be used and the specific purpose of the AI tool or system that will be used; and (ii) the patient or the patient's representative provides consent to the permitted use of AI. A licensed professional that violates applicable requirements relating to the use of AI is subject to discipline under the Uniform Disciplinary Act. "Permitted use of AI" is defined to mean the use of AI tools or systems by a licensed professional to assist in providing administrative support or supplementary support in therapy or psychotherapy services where the licensed professional maintains full responsibility for all interactions, outputs, and data use associated with the system and satisfies other requirements in the bill. Unauthorized Therapy Services . An individual, corporation, or entity is prohibited from offering therapy or psychotherapy services to the public, including through the use of internet-based AI, unless the services are conducted by a licensed professional. A violation of this requirement is deemed to affect the public interest and to be an unfair or deceptive act in trade or commerce for the purpose of applying the Consumer Protection Act.

HB 2615.digest: Voluntary Disclosure Agreement Program . Beginning July 1, 2027, the DOR VDA program is codified and limited to the B&O tax. To qualify for the program, taxpayers must: disclose all relevant taxable activity to the DOR; not engage in fraud, evasion, or misrepresentation in reporting tax liabilities; not have been directly contacted by the DOR for enforcement purposes; and meet any other application requirements set forth by the DOR. The DOR is authorized to rescind a VDA within one year of its application if a business is found to have misrepresented or falsified any information on its application. Tax Amnesty . A tax amnesty program is established beginning June 10, 2026. All penalties and interest are waived for the B&O, PUT, and state and local sales and use tax liabilities required to be reported and paid before July 1, 2026. This includes taxes billed by the DOR or disclosed by the taxpayer on or after July 1, 2026.

HB 2616.digest: Food Security and Surplus Crop Recovery . Harvest Assistance Account . The Harvest Assistance Account is created in the custody of the State Treasurer. The account consists of receipts directed to the account from legislative appropriations, gifts, grants, and donations. Expenditures may be used only to support rapid response to severe weather or market disruptions to harvest. Only the Director of the Department of Agriculture (WSDA) or the Director's designee may authorize expenditures. Convening of Agencies . The WSDA must convene the Department of Enterprise Services, the Department of Corrections, and the Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction to develop a strategy to expand institutional purchasing of Washington-grown food. The strategy must prioritize purchasing for state agencies, corrections facilities, and public schools. The WSDA must submit the strategy in the form of a report to the Legislature by December 1, 2028. Exemption from Producer Responsibility Requirements . Packaging used to store perishable agricultural products is added to the exempt materials from the producer responsibility requirements for covered packaging and paper products, until the Department of Ecology (Ecology) determines that commercially viable alternatives are reasonably available. Climate and Energy . An exemption in the Climate Commitment Act (CCA) is modified for motor vehicle fuel or special fuel that is used exclusively for agricultural purposes by a farm fuel user, to remove the provision that, beginning January 1, 2030, the exemption only applies to motor vehicle fuel or special fuel that the farm fuel user uses to propel a motor vehicle, so it would continue to apply whether the motor vehicle fuel or special fuel is used to propel a motor vehicle or not. An exemption to coverage in the CCA program is added for emissions from the combustion, oxidation, other process, or end use of a lubricant. This exemption applies regardless of whether a supplier demonstrates to Ecology that a lubricant is not combusted or oxidized. It is provided that the provisions of the law relating to hydrofluorocarbons and emissions reductions, including the requirement to participate in the Refrigerant Management Program or to meet specific global warming potential limits, do not apply to substitutes, refrigerants, or equipment used in agricultural production or food storage. Ecology must administer a grant program for the purpose of performing equipment retrofits necessary to protect food quality and storage capacity. Ecology may adopt rules to administer the grant program. The Agricultural Refrigeration Transition Account (ART Account) is created in the State Treasury. The ART Account consists of legislative appropriations, gifts, grants, and donations. Moneys in the account may be spent only after appropriation. Expenditures from the account may be used only for capital grants for cold storage retrofits to protect food quality and capacity. Studies, Analyses, and Reports . Agricultural Tax Incentives Study and Report . The WSDA and Washington State University (WSU) must complete a study on agricultural tax incentives in other states in order to identify potential options for additional agricultural tax incentives in Washington. At a minimum, the study must analyze tax incentives pertaining to farm equipment purchasing, including equipment with emissions-reducing technology and equipment used in precision agriculture. HB 2629.digest: Scrap Metal Businesses . It is unlawful to sell or offer for sale transaction records involving nonferrous metal property. Transactions involving nonferrous metal property may not be made with cash and may only be paid with a stored value device, electronic funds transfer, other electronic payment method, or a nontransferable check. A scrap metal business may pay up to a maximum of $30 in a stored value device or electronic funds transfer for nonferrous metal property. The limitations in transaction methods do not apply to transactions between commercial accounts. Civil penalties are established for a scrap metal business who engages in a pledge for, purchase of, or the trade of stolen copper that was used in telecommunications cable. A first violation is up to $10,000, a second violation is up to $20,000, and a third violation must result in loss of licensure. A scrap metal business that commits three violations must immediately surrender their license. Criminal Offense Established for Destruction of Critical Communications Infrastructure . Destruction of critical communications infrastructure is established as criminal profiteering as a class C felony ranked at a seriousness level II. A person is guilty of destruction of critical communications infrastructure if, with intent to cause damage, commit theft, or cause harm to communications infrastructure, including both physical and cyber components that deliver voice, video, and data services, the person causes damage to or renders inoperable such voice, video, or data services. In addition, a person who sustains injury to their person, business, or property by a person committing destruction of critical communications infrastructure may file an action against the perpetrator for the recovery of damages and reasonable attorney's fees and costs.

These agencies must work in partnership with Washington Technology Solutions (WaTech) and Your Washington to ensure that customer service delivery channels meet enterprise accessibility, usability, and customer experience best practices and prioritize digital-first services. As soon as practicable, these agencies must begin partnering with WaTech to move towards a "one front door" vision of state digital services accessible in a single place. The OSOS, the WDFW, and the OIC websites and digital applications should prominently display a standardized navigational component that provides a clear pathway to WA.gov, and the agencies must collaborate with WaTech to develop a schedule for integrating their digital applications with WA.gov. Reporting Requirements. By October 8, 2026, the OSOS, the WDFW, and the OIC must provide Your Washington with a report detailing: customer experience metrics, including data related to timelines, communications, and outcomes for delivering public services; information about customer feedback and complaints and a summary of the most common customer complaints; a description of the agency's delivery of digital and in-person services, and identification of areas for improvement; and policies to strengthen plain language writing and design principles, including the extent to which the agency's policies or practices align with Executive Order 23-02. HB 2632.digest: "Noncitizen" is defined as an individual who is not a citizen or national of the United States. "Nonimmigrant citizen" is defined as a person that meets the definition of "nonimmigrant alien" under the Immigration and Nationality Act. Using "Noncitizen" in State and Local Statutes and Official Documents . Except where required by federal law or necessary to comply with federal requirements that are a prescribed condition to the allocation of federal funds to the state, all state and local government statutes, codes, rules, regulations, and other official documents enacted after July 1, 2026, must use the term "noncitizen" or other context-appropriate term, instead of the term "alien," when referring to an individual who is not a citizen or national of the United States. All state and local entities are urged to review their statutes, codes, rules, regulations, and other official documents and revise them to omit the use of the term "alien" when referring to an individual who is not a citizen or national of the United States. Expedited Rulemaking. A state agency may use the expedited rulemaking process if the proposed rule only substitutes the term "alien," when used to refer to an individual who is not a citizen or national of the United States, with the term "noncitizen" or other context-appropriate term and makes necessary grammatical changes and definitions resulting from the substitution, but does not change the effect of the rule. An agency may proceed with entering an order adopting the rule without further notice or public hearing even if the agency receives written objections to the rule. Replacing "Alien" with "Noncitizen" in State Law . Except where required by federal law or necessary to comply with federal requirements that are a prescribed condition to the allocation of federal funds to the state, the term "alien" is replaced with the term "noncitizen." In certain instances, references to the term "alien" are replaced with "person who is not a citizen or national of the United States" to conform with the original meaning of the statute. References to the term "alien" are not replaced with the term "noncitizen" where: use of the term is required by federal law or necessary to comply with federal requirements that are a prescribed condition to the allocation of federal funds to the state; or the term is used to describe a nonhuman entity. When Required to Comply with Federal Law or Funding Requirements. The following references, where use of the term "alien" is required to comply with federal law or funding requirements, are not revised: "United States issued alien number"; "ATF-6 NIA Application and Permit for Temporary Importation of Firearms and Ammunition by Nonimmigrant Aliens"; "qualified alien," where required to be consistent with federal immigration law or funding requirements; "nonimmigrant alien" and "nonresident alien," where required to be consistent with federal labor law or funding requirements; and

HB 2640.digest: The Department may refuse to accept an initial or amended financing statement for filing if it was not filed by a trusted filer and the Department reasonably believes that the record was communicated to the Department with the intent to harass or defraud the person identified as the debtor. If the record is subsequently accepted based on additional information, the record is effective as if it was not initially refused, except as against a purchaser of the collateral that reasonably relied upon the absence of the record. A "trusted filer" is a person that regularly causes records to be communicated to the filing office through batch filing and has provided the office with current contact information and information sufficient to establish the person's identity. A process is created for termination of a wrongfully filed financing statement. The Department may file a termination statement with respect to a financing statement if it receives an affidavit from a person identified as the debtor in the financing statement indicating that the filed record was not authorized and was communicated to the Department with the intent to harass or defraud the debtor. The affidavit must contain specified information and be signed under penalty of perjury. The Department may reject an affidavit that it believes was delivered with the intent to harass or defraud the secured party. If the financing statement that is the subject of the affidavit was submitted by a trusted filer, the Department must first conduct an expedited administrative review to determine whether it was submitted with intent to harass or defraud the debtor. A filed termination statement is not effective until 30 days after it is filed. The Department must notify the secured party under the financing statement that the termination statement has been filed and will become effective 30 days after filing. Notice must be sent by certified mail on the day the termination statement is filed, with a copy sent to the electronic mail address provided by the secured party. Before a termination statement takes effect, a secured party who believes the filed record was authorized may request that the Department conduct an expedited review of the filed record and any provided documentation. Based on the expedited review, the Department may remove the filed termination statement from the record and conduct an administrative review. If the Department determines after an administrative review that the financing statement was submitted with intent to harass or defraud the debtor, the Department must promptly file a termination statement, which takes effect immediately, and send notice of the termination to the secured party. The secured party may file an action against the Department seeking reinstatement of a terminated financing statement. The action must be filed no later than six months after the date on which the termination statement takes effect. If the court determines the financing statement was authorized and not communicated with the intent to harass or defraud the debtor, the court must order reinstatement of the financing statement. If the court finds that the filed record was communicated with the intent to harass or defraud the debtor, the Department and the debtor may recover from the secured party their costs and reasonable attorneys' fees incurred in the action. HB 2645.digest: The failure and permanent closure of the Fairfax Bridge is declared an emergency that requires immediate attention. The WSDOT is directed to expedite the restoration of the Fairfax Bridge on SR 165, across the Carbon River. The Secretary of the WSDOT (Secretary) is granted emergency authority to expedite the process of replacing the Fairfax Bridge, including by waiving or suspending statutory obligations or limitations in the following areas: liability for participation in interlocal agreements; inspection fees owed to the Department of Labor and Industries; regulations, tariffs, and notice requirements under the jurisdiction of the Utilities and Transportation Commission; and application of tax due dates and penalties relating to collection of taxes. The Secretary is also granted emergency authority to expedite the process of bridge replacement by waiving or suspending other statutory and regulatory obligations or limitations prescribing the procedures for the conduct of state business, or the orders, rules, or regulations of any state agency, if strict compliance with the provision of any statute, order, rule, or regulation would in any way prevent, hinder, or delay necessary action in coping with the emergency. This authority would not apply if the waiver or suspension would conflict with federal requirements that are a prescribed condition to the allocation of federal funds to the state, or the waiver or suspension would conflict with the rights, under the First Amendment, of freedom of speech or of the people to peaceably assemble. The Secretary is required to give as much notice as practical to the Governor, legislative leadership of the transportation committees, and impacted local governments when issuing orders pursuant to the granted emergency authority. Activities and projects performed pursuant to House Bill 2645 are not subject to any of the provisions of Executive Order 25-07.

The bill clarifies that a recipient of a conditional certificate for the deferral must apply to DOR for a tax deferral certificate before the initiation of the construction. HB 2655.digest: An exemption from sales and use tax is established for sales of eligible server equipment to be installed, without intervening use, in eligible computer data centers, and to charges for labor and services to install such equipment, subject to certain requirements. This exemption also applies to sales of eligible power infrastructure, and related labor and services to construct, install, repair, alter, or improve such infrastructure at an eligible data center, subject to certain requirements. This exemption expires July 1, 2048. Eligible Computer Data Centers . "Eligible computer data center" means a computer data center: (1) located in a county east of the Cascades that borders another state and has a population of at least 500,000 persons; (2) having at least 20,000 square feet dedicated to housing working servers; and (3) for which the commencement of construction occurs after June 30, 2026, and before July 1, 2035. "Computer data center" means a facility comprised of one or more buildings, which may be comprised of multiple businesses constructed specifically and used primarily to house working servers, where the facility has the following characteristics: (1) uninterruptible power supplies, generator backup power, or both; (2) sophisticated fire suppression and prevention systems; and (3) enhanced physical security, such as: access to the facility restricted to selected personnel; permanent security guards; video camera surveillance; an electronic system requiring passcodes, keycards, or biometric scans, such as hand scans and retinal or fingerprint recognition; or similar security features. A facility comprised of one building or more than one building must have a combined square footage of at least 100,000 square feet. Exemption Certificates . This exemption applies to eligible data centers for which an exemption certificate has been issued by the Department of Revenue (DOR). Exemption certificates expire two years after the date of issuance, unless construction has been commenced. No new exemption certificates may be issued on or after July 1, 2036. Construction Requirement . To qualify for the sales tax exemption under this act, a qualifying business or tenant must certify to the DOR that, for new construction work to be performed on the site of the computer data center, the computer data center receiving an exemption will be constructed by the prime contractor and its subcontractors in a way that includes community workforce agreements or project labor agreements and the payment of area standard prevailing wages and apprenticeship utilization requirements, subject to certain conditions. The minimum number of family wage employment positions must be maintained while the exemption certificate is valid. "Family wage employment positions" must meet the following standards. HB 2660.digest: If a child is under age 5 at the time of filing a dependency petition and the court releases the child to the care of a parent, guardian, or legal custodian following a shelter care hearing, the court may order the parent, guardian, or legal custodian to comply with the least restrictive conditions necessary to maintain the safety of the child in the home if the court finds that there is reasonable cause to believe that these conditions are necessary to maintain the safety of the child. Any of these conditions that are ordered must be reviewed by the court at least every 30 days to determine whether the conditions are still necessary to maintain the safety of the child. If the court ordered conditions described above involve the participation of the parent, guardian, or legal custodian in a service or evaluation, the parent, guardian, or legal custodian must sign a release of information allowing the Department of Children, Youth, and Families (DYCF) to make a referral and receive any related results and the DCYF must provide all necessary referrals to that service or evaluation within seven days of signing this release. Failure by the DYCF to provide timely referrals or access to service conditions may not be used as a basis for removal, continued shelter care, or a finding of dependency. The court may only order the conditions described above that the DYCF identifies as: culturally appropriate; consistent with and in compliance with the state and federal Indian Child Welfare Acts; reasonably available to the parent, guardian, or legal custodian; and reasonably accessible to the parent, guardian, or legal custodian. The fact that the parent participated in prevention services, safety planning, or conditions necessary to maintain the safety of the child under the conditions described above may not be construed as an admission of abuse or neglect during a dependency fact-finding hearing. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: The substitute bill modifies the conditions that the court is authorized to order in the underlying bill to require that these conditions are: the least restrictive conditions necessary to maintain the safety of the child in the home; reviewed every thirty days to determine whether the conditions are still necessary to maintain the safety of the child in the home; and identified by the Department of Children, Youth, and Families as consistent with and in compliance with the state and federal Indian Child Welfare Acts.

HB 2668.digest: Relocation Plan . The Department of Fish and Wildlife (WDFW) must identify one or more alternate locations suitable for the relocation of the WDFW-owned and operated pheasant rearing and release facility located in Lewis County commonly known as the Bob Oke Game Farm (Game Farm) that do not pose a material risk of contaminating municipal or residential drinking water supplies, first determining if property the WDFW currently owns or manages is suitable for relocation. The WDFW must submit the list of properties to the committees of the House and Senate with jurisdiction over the capital budget and the legislators representing the legislative district in which the Game Farm is located. The WDFW must request funding in the 2027-29 Capital Budget for predesign to: evaluate each candidate site's proximity to certain water sources and the potential operational impacts on water supplies; consider access, infrastructure needs, land availability, zoning and land use compatibility, and the ability to maintain wildlife management and release functions; consult with affected local governments, water utilities, tribes, and conservation districts; and estimate costs, timelines, and logistical requirements for relocation. At the conclusion of the predesign, the WDFW must submit a relocation report to the Governor and appropriate committees of the Legislature that includes a recommendation for a preferred site and certain other information related to a schedule and cost estimates for relocation. Once a preferred location has been identified, the WDFW must submit a request for funding needed to relocate the Game Farm the in 2029-31 Capital Budget, and must continue to seek funding until the Game Farm has been relocated. Remediation Plan . The WDFW must request funding in the 2027-29 Capital Budget to complete design work to remediate the current Game Farm site. The remediation plan must address continued groundwater and soil monitoring, prevention of further nitrate or nutrient leaching to groundwater, evaluation of restoration techniques to reduce existing nutrient concentrations. Once the design work is complete, the WDFW must submit a request for funding in the 2029-31 Capital Budget to fully remediate the current site, and must continue to seek funding until the site is fully remediated.

HB 2685.digest: When using or sharing tribal data, the state agencies that are members of the Governor's Indian Health Advisory Council (GIHAC) must do so in a manner consistent with tribal data sovereignty principles. These agencies are: the Health Care Authority, the Department of Children, Youth, and Families, the Department of Commerce, the Department of Corrections, the Department of Health, the Department of Social and Health Services, the Office of the Insurance Commissioner, the Office of the Superintendent of Public Instruction, and the Washington Health Benefit Exchange. The designated agencies must apply the following tribal data sovereignty principles: Tribes must have the same or enhanced access to state data as other public health jurisdictions and nongovernmental entities to carry out their governmental duties. Tribes must possess sovereign authority to manage the collection, ownership, application, and interpretation of their own data even when it is collected by federal, state, or local governments, or third parties. Tribes must retain an ownership interest in their data even when the data is located in state, federal, or other datasets, and this interest remains when the data is aggregated with other data. Unless otherwise required by law, tribes have the right to informed consent on how their data, including protected health information about tribal members, is used or shared with third parties. State agencies must meaningfully consult and engage with tribes, in accordance with their government-to-government relationship, on how and when to share, analyze, report, or interpret tribal data. The designated agencies must include tribal data sovereignty principles in data sharing agreements. When developing tribal data sharing agreements, the agencies must refer to the GIHAC tribal data sharing agreement checklist. The agencies must seek input and guidance from the GIHAC tribal data sovereignty committee on issues related to tribal data. The State Board of Health must adopt rules requiring health care providers, health care facilities, laboratories, and other required entities to report notifiable conditions to tribal health jurisdictions in Washington where the patient resides or, in the event the patient's residence cannot be determined, the tribal health department in which the patient received treatment. The adopted rules must require notification to tribal health jurisdictions wherever notification is required to local health jurisdictions. The rules must be adopted by July 31, 2027. Tribal data prepared, owned, used, or retained by the designated state agencies or by local health jurisdictions is exempt from public disclosure under the Public Records Act. "Tribal data" means data or information that is specific to an individual tribe and includes public or private data or information on or about a tribe or its people subject to tribal rights of ownership and control. Tribal data also includes, but is not limited to: tribal membership; tribal affiliation, events, and conditions within the tribe's jurisdiction and lands; information about tribal members and any persons living within the tribe's jurisdiction; tribal census tract; tribal land; and identification of tribal facilities, entities, and enterprises; and any individuals they serve. HB 2689.digest: Working Connections Child Care Program Eligibility . Eligibility for the WCCC program is modified so that income eligibility is maintained at 60 percent of the SMI, instead of increasing to 75 percent of the SMI beginning July 1, 2029, and 85 percent of the SMI (subject to funding) beginning July 1, 2031. Working Connections Child Care Subsidy Rates . Child care subsidy base rates are set at the seventy-fifth percentile of market, beginning July 1, 2027, for licensed or certified child care providers. Beginning with the 2028 MRS, a child care subsidy rate region must achieve a provider response rate of at least 40 percent and also be greater than the response rate for that region in the prior MRS for the results to be valid for the purpose of informing future rate increases for that region. A minimum of 65 percent participation must be achieved for a valid survey once a region achieves 65 percent. The DCYF is prohibited from allowing child care providers to receive a child care subsidy rate that is different than the rate for the subsidy region in which the provider is located. Working Connections Child Care Subsidy Payments . The DCYF must adopt rules that allow child care providers to claim daily subsidy payments as follows: for a child who has attended for 16 or more days in a calendar month, a provider may claim payment for the full number of authorized days; for a child who has attended 9 to 15 days in a calendar month, a provider may claim payment for the full number of authorized days, or for 15 days, whichever is fewer; and for a child who has attended 1 to 8 days in a calendar month, a provider may claim payment for the full number of authorized days, or for 11 days, whichever is fewer. Daily subsidy payments must be paid in half-day or partial-day rates, as established in rule, for a child authorized for and receiving half-day or partial-day care. The requirement that the DCYF pay child care providers prospectively based on when child care is expected to begin is repealed.

HB 2711.digest: Fuel Taxes . Fuel taxes received attributable to the aggregated inflationary adjustments to the component tax rates are distributed in the same manner as the other 2025 increases in the motor fuel tax and special fuel tax rates. Retail Sales and Use Taxes on Acquisitions of Luxury Vehicles, and Recreational Vessels . The use tax bases for the luxury vehicle tax and recreational vessel tax are modified to align with the corresponding sales tax bases, prohibiting the value of any trade-in from being deducted from the measure of tax. Various technical updates are made. Motor homes are exempted from the sales and use taxes on luxury vehicles for the period July 1, 2026, through December 31, 2026. Several changes are made to the retail sales and use taxes on luxury vehicles. In the case of a lease requiring periodic payments, the tax may be remitted in equal periodic payments over the term of the lease. The exemptions available under the general retail sales and use tax to enrolled tribal members and to nonresidents are extended to the sales and use taxes on luxury vehicles. Motor vehicle dealers are exempt from penalties and interest on any unpaid tax due for the tax reporting periods through June 30, 2026. Luxury Aircraft Tax . The additional 10 percent luxury tax on non-commercial aircraft, which would otherwise take effect on April 1, 2026, is repealed in its entirety. Aircraft Fuel Tax . On November 1, 2026, the current aircraft fuel tax is increased from 18 cents per gallon to 25 cents per gallon. The 7 cent increase will be deposited into the newly established Sustainable Aviation Fuel Airport Infrastructure Account created in the state treasury. Aircraft Registration Fee . Beginning January 1, 2027, the annual aircraft registration fee is increased from $15 to $30. The aircraft registration fee is increased annually by 2 percent beginning January 1, 2028. Increased revenue from the fee increase must be deposited in the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Account. Aircraft Excise Tax . Beginning on January 1, 2026, annual excise taxes by aircraft type are raised by a range of $70 to $1,095, increasing excise taxes due to a range of $120 to $1,220, depending on aircraft type. Beginning on January 1, 2028, the aircraft excise taxes are increased by 2 percent each year. The increased amount, including the 2 percent annual adjustment, is deposited into the Sustainable Aviation Fuel Account. Commercial unpiloted aircraft systems are made subject to the annual aircraft excise tax. Sustainable Aviation Fuel Airport Infrastructure Account . The Sustainable Aviation Fuel Airport Infrastructure Account is created in the state treasury. Twenty-eight percent of the revenue collected from aircraft fuel taxes by the WSDOT must be deposited in this account. These funds are subject to appropriation and can be used only for activities at airports supporting sustainable aviation fuel infrastructure improvement and sustainable aviation fuel infrastructure preservation projects. Tire Fee . The amount of the tire fee that a retailer is allowed to retain is clarified to be 25 cents per tire. Registered Tow Truck Operators and the Department of Licensing Reimbursement Program for Tows of Indigent Persons' Vehicles . The program to reimburse RTTOs for the costs of towing indigent persons' vehicles is delayed to July 1, 2027. Clean Alternative Fuel Vehicle Report . HB 2718.digest: Permitting . Once it is determined that a project will need a particular permit and the parameters thereof, WSDOT multiagency permit program staff (Staff) must ensure, to the maximum extent possible, that a meeting with the appropriate federal or state agency or agencies responsible for the issuance of the permit occurs within 30 days. The meeting must develop methods by which the issuance of the permit may be expedited, and the Staff is responsible for the implementation of any such methods. The Staff must, to the maximum extent possible, ensure that within 90 days of the occurrence of a meeting regarding a permit, a decision is reached regarding the issuance of the permit. Within 30 days of determining that a project will need to receive a particular permit and the relevant parameters of the permit, the Staff must begin soliciting community input regarding the permit, including from impacted cities, counties, and federally recognized tribes. Cities, counties, and federally recognized tribes must also be included in any outreach and meetings regarding the permit. If no comments regarding HPA permits, shoreline permits, SEPA permits, or wastewater discharge permits are made, by the agency responsible for the issuance of such permits, within 60 days of the submission of the permit application, the permit is deemed approved. Any comments by an agency responsible for the issuance of such a permit must be based on objective written standards. If comments regarding a permit are made, the Staff may resubmit the permit with such modifications as are necessary to resolve the comment or comments. If no further comments are received, within 30 days of the resubmission of the permit application, the permit is deemed approved. If all comments regarding a permit have been addressed according to the objective written standards of that agency and no permit has been issued, the Staff may make a finding that: all comments regarding a permit have been addressed; and a reasonable person would find that any comments that have not been addressed are extraneous or irrelevant to the objective written standards of the agency, and the permit is deemed approved. As part of their efforts to streamline permitting, the Staff must collaborate with, and ensure input from, impacted federally recognized tribes. Such collaboration and input must be solicited as early as is feasible, and continue throughout the process of obtaining permits. Permitting Report . The WSDOT is required to develop a report regarding the following items: templates for permit approval based upon each permitting agencies' policies, for use by state agencies and local governments; emergency provisions that allow for expedited project construction, which may be implemented during periods of nonemergency, and incorporating that work into ongoing permitting processes; opportunities to simplify funding sources and best distribute federal resources to maximize timely project delivery; a plan for centralizing communication and current information on the progress of issuing any permit; processes for identifying points of contact within each permitting agency for a given permit and the individual responsible for communicating any staff changes; recommendations for changing the process allowing permit exemptions; and plans for programmatic permits based upon project type and tools available to maximize efficiency in permit approval for projects. HB 2720.digest: Specified health plans must pay a covered lives assessment beginning in calendar year 2027. Covered lives for purposes of the assessment are individuals residing in Washington that are enrolled in health coverage offered by: self-funded multiple employer welfare arrangements; public or private employer-sponsored self-funded group health plans or Taft-Hartley Trust health plans; and health plans offered by health carriers (collectively referred to as covered entities). The assessment is calculated on a per member per month basis and is initially set at 58 cents. The assessment must be updated every two years based on an adjustment factor composed of changes in rates of inflation and population. The rate increase may be no more than 10 percent. The Office of the Insurance Commissioner (Commissioner) must calculate the assessment, notify covered entities of their payment obligations, and determine a schedule for receipt no more frequently than quarterly. Covered entities must provide the Commissioner with the information needed to calculate the covered entity's number of covered lives. Payments are due within 45 days of notification and provisions for interest and penalties for late payment are established. A covered entity that fails to pay the covered lives assessment within 90 days must be assessed a penalty of 150 percent of the assessment owed and the Commissioner may revoke a health carrier's certificate of authority or registration, which may not be reissued until all assessments, penalties, and interest are fully paid. The Behavioral Health Emergency Services Account (Account) is created in the State Treasury and requires appropriation. All receipts from the assessment, including interest and penalties, must be deposited into the Account. Expenditures from the Account may be used only for the following behavioral health emergency services administered through BH-ASOs or federally recognized tribes: crisis stabilization units; 23-hour crisis relief centers; agencies certified by the DOH to provide outpatient crisis services; and mobile rapid response crisis teams. The Account may also be used for some administrative costs associated with implementation of the act and refunds of erroneous payments. The Account may not be used for reimbursement of services provided to individuals enrolled in the Medicaid program or for services that have been directly billed by a provider or on the provider's behalf and reimbursed by a covered entity or payer for the covered entity or payer's enrollee. A BH-ASO, federally recognized tribe, health care provider, or health care entity that receives funds from the Account may not bill a covered entity for a behavioral health emergency service listed above provided to a covered life. When determining the adequacy of a health carrier's provider network, beginning January 1, 2027, a carrier that has paid their covered lives assessment is deemed to have an adequate provider network for the behavioral health emergency services listed above. The Commissioner must adopt rules and undertake actions necessary to implement the assessment. The Commissioner, in consultation with specified agencies and entities, must revise existing rules to support transitioning payment for the services to the prospective covered lives assessment, including rules related to network access; alternate access delivery requests; contracting; and claims payments. The Health Care Authority (Authority) must adopt rules and undertake action

HB 2721.digest: State Board of Architects and Registered Commercial Interior Designers . The State Board of Architects is expanded to include authority over the practice of commercial interior designers and is renamed to the State Board for Architects and Registered Commercial Interior Designers (Board). The Board membership is increased to nine members, two of whom must be registered commercial interior designers who are residents and have at least eight years' experience in responsible charge of the practice or teaching of registered commercial interior design. For initial appointments, a registered commercial interior designer may qualify with equivalent professional experience in commercial interior design prior to the establishment of the registration system, as determined by the Board. The executive director has oversight authority over the Board. Registered architects may qualify for a Board appointment with five years' experience, rather than eight. Qualification Requirements for Registered Commercial Interior Designers . An applicant applying for a certificate of registration to engage in the practice of registered commercial interior design must be of good moral character, at least 18 years of age, and submit the following: a completed and signed written application in the form prescribed by the Board; evidence of graduation and receipt of a degree from an approved educational program; evidence indicating the successful completion of experience deemed necessary by the Board; evidence of the successful completion of the National Council for Interior Design Qualification examination administered by Council for Interior Design Qualification; evidence of the successful completion of a Washington State Law Review Examination for Registered Commercial Interior Designers, as established by the Board; and payment of all applicable fees. Certificates of registration may be granted to an applicant who pays the registration fee and who: is a registered commercial interior designer in another state or territory of the United States, the District of Columbia, or another country; has equivalent qualifications and experience as determined by the Board; and provides evidence of successful completion of the Washington State Law Review Examination for Registered Commercial Interior Designers. Architects . Architects with certification or authorization to practice in the state are eligible for registration as a commercial interior designer, subject to approval of a completed application and fee submission. Licensed architects are not required to register as a commercial interior designer to practice as such, but must obtain registration in order to use the title of "registered commercial interior designer." An architect registered as a commercial interior designer who satisfies the requirements for licensure renewal as an architect also satisfies the requirements for renewal of the registration as a commercial interior designer. Certificate of Registration and Seal Issuance . The Board's director must issue a certificate of registration to any applicant who has met all requirements and paid the applicable fee. Each registrant must obtain a seal of the design authorized by the Board bearing the registered commercial interior designer's name, registration number, the title of "registered commercial interior designer," and the state. HB 2730.digest: Beginning with its review of the aerospace tax incentives due by December 1, 2029, the JLARC must specifically assess the share of aerospace industry employment in Washington in comparison with other states based on a rolling five-year average. To the best of its ability, the JLARC must consider and report on whether Washington's share of aerospace industry employment was significantly impacted by changes in noncommercial aerospace sectors. The JLARC must also consider large changes in employment for different types of jobs across different aerospace sectors and any changing economic conditions. The Legislature intends to extend the expiration dates of the aerospace tax incentives if a review finds that the share of aerospace industry employment in Washington stays the same or grows relative to other states.
HB 2730.digest_source: WA House Bill Analysis 2026 (Summary of Bill)
HB 2730.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to clarifying the metric for judging the effectiveness of aerospace tax preferences;
HB 2730.title: Aerospace tax preferences

Granville , the United States Supreme Court recognized parental rights as a fundamental liberty interest, yet declined to set a standard of review. It is specified that the Legislature intends for chapter 26.09 RCW to be implemented subject to a constitutional floor that consists of several principles, including: a presumption of parental fitness; equal standing for similarly situated parents; any intrusion on the parent-child relationship must be the least restrictive to parental rights; a parental duty to cooperate; and the requirement that court orders must be clear and contestable. The bill may be known and cited as Troxel II.

HB 2745.digest: The insurance premium tax on qualifying insurers is increased from 2 percent to 2.75 percent for premiums, premium deposits, and prepayments collected during calendar year 2026. The portion of any taxes collected that exceeds 2 percent of premiums and prepayments must be deposited in the state Health Care Affordability account and used to fund the premium assistance and cost-sharing reduction program. The portion of any taxes collected that exceeds 2 percent of premiums and prepayments must be borne solely by the taxpayer and may not be passed through to enrollees in premiums, rates, plan design, or otherwise, unless the Insurance Commissioner (Commissioner) determines that to do so would create a significant risk of carrier insolvency or consumer harm. A taxpayer must demonstrate the taxpayer's compliance with this requirement as directed by the Commissioner. The Commissioner may adopt rules to implement this requirement.
HB 2745.digest_source: WA House Bill Analysis 2026 (Summary of Bill)
HB 2745.legal_title: AN ACT Relating to temporarily increasing insurance premium taxes on insurers to fund health insurance premium assistance;

HB 2747.digest: For the 2027-29 and 2029-31 fiscal biennia, estimated resources to be used in determining compliance with the four-year balanced budget requirement must be based solely on beginning NGF-O fund balances, forecasted NGF-O revenues, and adjustments for legislation. The current alternative calculation for forecasted revenues, using the greater of the forecasted revenues or the prior biennium's second-year forecast increased by 4.5 percent per fiscal year, does not apply during these biennia. This modification applies to budgets proposed by the Governor and those adopted by the Legislature during this period. Substitute Bill Compared to Original Bill: The substitute bill clarifies that during the 2027-29 and 2029-31 fiscal biennia, the official revenue forecast shall be used when calculating available funds for all NGF-O funds rather than for just the State General Fund.
HB 2747.digest_source: WA House Bill Report (Summary of Bill)
